stories.title: Libor Alois Schlesinger (1806–1893): the barricades of Prague
stories.group: A rebel of 1848, a wagon train to Denver, and a ranch on the Fountain
stories.html:
Libor Schlesinger (1806–1893) in his Denver years, probably the early 1880s. The oval halftone looks like a printed plate, perhaps the portrait that ran with his 1886 Květy Americké biography or his 1893 Pokrok západu obituary.

Libor was born on 19 October 1806 in Ústí nad Orlicí (in German, Wildenschwert), a weaving town in eastern Bohemia, then part of the Austrian Empire. His father, also named Libor, was a glazier and carpenter who also dealt in linen thread, and his grandfather Godhard had been a glazier too. His mother, Barbora Andres, was a weaver's daughter; she died young and left four girls and two boys. Libor went to school in Ústí and at a German school in nearby Hilbaty until he was 11, had a tutor until 14, and then learned to weave. As a journeyman he worked in Šternberk, in Moravia, and in Vienna. Back home at about 20, he started his own cloth business, selling in Brno, Vienna and Prague, and by 1840 he was one of the big traders of the region, with warehouses in Ústí, Kutná Hora and Prague. On 13 February 1832 he married Anna Rypka, a weaver's daughter from house no. 177 in Ústí, one of ten children.

A rebel of 1848. Libor was a Czech patriot at a time when that could land a man in jail. Bohemia was ruled from Vienna, German was the language of government, and the newspapers were censored. Libor belonged to Svornost ("Concord"), the patriotic society around the journalist Karel Havlíček. When revolution swept across Europe in the spring of 1848, he was at the great public meeting in Prague on 11 March and was chosen for the delegation that carried the Czechs' demands to Emperor Ferdinand: equal rights for the Czech language and a constitution. In June, over the Pentecost holiday, Prague rose against the Austrian army. Libor fought on the barricades, was arrested on 12 June, and was held for months in the castle at Hradčany. Back home, Ústí elected him its deputy anyway. He quarreled with the town's dean and chaplain, and the police kept him under watch.

The banned books. In 1850 Libor traveled to Serbia, and on the way home he was arrested again, this time for bringing in Havlíček's forbidden writings. By the account in his 1893 obituary, the Prague paper Slovan reported in 1851 that a military court had sentenced him to six weeks in prison for distributing a book called Duch Národních novin ("The Spirit of the National News"), and the paper pointed out that the book wasn't even banned in Prague. The parish in Ústí twice had to issue copies of Libor's baptism record, in June 1847 and again in August 1848, probably for his election and his court cases. After all that, Libor moved out to Záměl, near Potštejn, where he had bought a mill, and it was there that his daughter Julia married the young miller Joseph Benesch.

To America. Libor's oldest son, Timothy, had already left for America in his teens, partly to stay out of the Austrian army. In November 1856, at 50, Libor followed. He sailed from Hamburg on the steamship Hammonia with Anna and three of their children, Mathilde, Anna and Sebald; the passenger list calls him a merchant. They took the train west and spent the first winter in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, where Timothy had been living for two years and where Joseph and Julia had arrived just two months before. "I wished to be near my children," Libor wrote.

Breaking prairie. In spring 1857 the family and a few other Bohemians from Cedar Rapids moved to Burt County, Nebraska, on the edge of the Omaha reservation about 60 miles north of Omaha, and started a little settlement along the stage road five miles south of Decatur. A 1929 history counts Libor among the very first Czech settlers in Nebraska. He had been a merchant all his life, so he hired help to build the house and break the sod, and his son-in-law Henry Reitze later teased that Libor never did master a team of oxen pulling a loaded wagon. Still, by 1860 he had 400 acres, 3 horses, 4 milk cows, 7 pigs and 6 oxen, and grew corn, buckwheat, hay, peas and potatoes, putting up 150 pounds of butter and 40 gallons of molasses that year. In the 1860 census Joseph Benesch was his next-door neighbor.

The flour business. In the fall of 1861 Libor and Henry Reitze had the local mill grind their wheat, loaded the flour into ox wagons and hauled it 600 miles to Denver to sell it themselves, cutting out the middleman. That first load didn't sell until spring, but Libor learned the trade fast. "I bought flour in Omaha at $3.00 per hundred pounds and sold it in Denver for $9.00, so there was some profit," he wrote. "I made several trips like that, buying and selling flour, butter, lard and eggs." One Christmas he got $25 for a hundred pounds of flour and $2.50 for a dozen "almost rotten" eggs. In the fall of 1862 Libor and Anna moved to Denver with the Reitzes, and that first winter the men earned $9 a load hauling firewood down from "the Pineries," 20 miles up Cherry Creek. In all he made five round trips by ox wagon over the Platte River Road.

The chief he had cured. On one early trip Libor met a Sioux man in such pain that he couldn't sit his horse. Libor doctored him for three days, and when they parted the man gave him a little cube and told him to show it to any Sioux he met. In the spring of 1864 Libor set out for Omaha one more time, to bring the rest of the family west, even though the Plains were at war. Anna rode a long way out with him to say goodbye, afraid she would never see him again, and he promised to write every week. On the road her letter caught up with him with news of the Hungate murders near Denver. Farther east he passed burned ranch houses and a dozen burned wagons, and "did not meet a living soul on the entire way." Camped about 45 miles from Fort Kearney, he was joined at his fire by warriors carrying stolen goods. Nobody spoke. Then a group of chiefs rode up, greeted him with a friendly "how," and told the others to go away, and among them was the man he had doctored. "I knew I was saved," Libor wrote. In the morning the chief helped him find and yoke his oxen.

At Fort Kearney the army wouldn't let the family go on until 20 wagons had gathered for protection. Libor, Timothy's and Joseph's families, three small children and two babies spent more than four months on the trail and reached Denver on 17 December 1864, two weeks after the Sand Creek Massacre. The next spring Libor and Joseph talked about one more freighting trip, but their wives talked them out of it.

Ranching on the Fountain. On the advice of John Eder, a friend from Vienna, Libor and Joseph went south looking for land and settled six miles apart on the east bank of Fountain Creek, on the old Cherokee Trail just south of the El Paso County line. They raised oats and corn, planted orchards, irrigated from the creek, and bought lame sheep from passing herders to build a flock. Libor ran 100 head of cattle and once spent a night out on the open prairie in the blizzard of March 1870. When he proved up his claim in 1874, two neighbors swore that he, his wife and children lived there in two houses, one adobe and one log, with a stable, four corrals, a milk house, a cellar and 35 acres under the plow. Spring floods in 1874 and 1875 turned the Fountain into "a roaring and foaming torrent" across his land, and his feet were failing, so at 70 he sold the cattle and the homestead and in 1877 moved to Denver. He grumbled that his family there had become too English, and he poured himself into some 70 letters and articles for the Czech papers Slavie and Pokrok západu. In about 1882 the Denver Czechs threw a party for the 50th anniversary of his engagement to Anna. A house fire on 20 December 1885 took nearly everything they owned. Anna died the next September, and Libor died on 24 February 1893 at Piñon Station, at 86. The Denver Republican called him "one of Colorado's oldest pioneers" and said he left thirty grandchildren. Joseph Benesch signed for the body, and the funeral left his daughter Mrs. Wise's house on Champa Street with a hearse and six carriages. A century later the Czech writer Otto Janka used him as the loose model for the hero of his boys' adventure novels about the Sioux.

Anna (Rypka) Schlesinger (1810–1886), Libor's wife of 54 years, in her later years in Colorado. She is buried in the same Denver lot as Libor; her stone reads "Aged 75 Yrs. 11 Mos."

Julia's sister Maria Anna, known as Anna, who married Billy Wise (labeled on MyHeritage). The upswept curls and deep lace jabot point to about 1875–1890.

Libor and Anna's children. Julia, our ancestor, married Joseph Benesch (below). Her brothers and sisters had Wild West lives of their own:

stories.title: Timothy Schlesinger (1834–1906): Burt County's young justice of the peace
stories.group: A rebel of 1848, a wagon train to Denver, and a ranch on the Fountain
stories.html: Timothy (1834–1906), the oldest, was a justice of the peace in Burt County before he was 30 and married Mary Peterson, a neighbor's daughter, in 1860. Libor's memoir says he rode as a first lieutenant of cavalry near Fort Kearney. From 1864 he ran grocery stores in the gold towns of Black Hawk and Central City and a wholesale grocery on Larimer Street in Denver, then went into lumber, supplying timber for the new mines and mills. He bought land with Libor and Sebald in what is now Golden Gate Canyon State Park, joined the Leadville silver boom in 1879, and built a house at 1544 Race Street in Denver that is now on the National Register of Historic Places. The silver crash of 1893 wiped him out, and he died of a stroke on Christmas Eve 1906 in a mining camp near Prescott, Arizona, still chasing a strike.

stories.title: Mathilda Schlesinger and Henry Reitze: Denver's first bakery
stories.group: A rebel of 1848, a wagon train to Denver, and a ranch on the Fountain
stories.html: Mathilda married Henry Reitze, a German baker who came to the gold fields in 1858. Henry was co-owner of the City Bakery in Auraria, Denver's first bakery; its ad was one of a dozen in the very first issue of the Rocky Mountain News on 23 April 1859, and a Methodist preacher remembered his "pies and milk, the like of which was not found in the cabin home." He lent his bread wagon as the cart for Denver's first hanging, built the only icehouse in town, and was a founding steward of what became Trinity Methodist Church. Back in Nebraska in 1860 he decided at 30 that he didn't want to be an old bachelor, heard about a family upriver with daughters, and rode up on the pretext of looking at land. "After I saw the girls I didn't want to see the land," he said. In the Cherry Creek flood of May 1864 he loaded Mathilda and the babies into a covered wagon and tied it to his old log cabin. He later ran a painting and wallpaper business and a hotel, and took the family to Germany for six months in 1887.

stories.title: Anna Schlesinger and Billy Wise: a saddler's dime-novel life
stories.group: A rebel of 1848, a wagon train to Denver, and a ranch on the Fountain
stories.html: Anna married William "Billy" Wise, a German saddler and army teamster whose life reads like a dime novel. He lived through a tornado that tore apart the army camps on the Cache la Poudre in 1857, cooked for a supply train to Utah, and reached the Pikes Peak gold fields in 1859 after a winter march on which men froze to death. He was named one of Denver City's first eight police officers in 1860 and fought with the Colorado Volunteers at Glorieta Pass. In 1864 his men voted to hang a soldier who had murdered a comrade; at the court-martial that followed, the officers found Billy guilty but asked that his sentence be remitted. After he married Anna in 1866 he ran "The National Park," a beer garden and road house on Champa Street with brass bands on Sundays, rode as a captain of the 1870 Big Horn gold expedition into Wyoming, and spent twenty years as a deputy sheriff who usually brought "his man to bay." Their house at 2630 Champa Street is where Libor's funeral began.

stories.title: Sebald Schlesinger (1843–1918): a bugler on the Platte River Road
stories.group: A rebel of 1848, a wagon train to Denver, and a ranch on the Fountain
stories.html:
Sebald (1843–1918), the youngest son, stayed behind in 1862 to join the Nebraska cavalry as a bugler, then served as a sergeant patrolling the Platte River Road. In August 1864 a bullet grazed his scalp in a skirmish, and that September his father met him on the trail near Fort Kearney. He married Hannah Christopherson, a Swedish immigrant, and moved to Black Hawk and then Golden, where he owned a saloon, led the Golden Brass Band and Schlessinger's Quadrille Orchestra ("good music guaranteed"), and rode the new fire engine "Fire King" up the canyon to fight the great Central City fire of 1874. He later farmed in Arizona, taught piano in Denver, and died at the soldiers' home in Monte Vista.

Sources: his 1806 birth register; his own memoir "Czech Freighter of the Sixties"; his 1886 biography in Květy americké, published in his lifetime; Rose Rosicky, A History of Czechs (Bohemians) in Nebraska (1929); Nancy K. Prince, "Freighter, Baker, Music Maker" (2013), and her research notes, which include the 2007 Hrnčiřík parish research and the 1874 homestead file.

stories.title: Joseph Benesch (1830–1917) and Julia Schlesinger: four months on the plains
stories.group: A rebel of 1848, a wagon train to Denver, and a ranch on the Fountain
stories.html:
Joseph Benesch, the miller's son from Kutná Hora who brought his family across the plains to Colorado in 1864.

Julia (Schlesinger) Benesch, Libor's daughter, who died in Pueblo in 1915. The brooch and lace-edged collar suggest the 1880s.

Joseph was born on 9 March 1830 in house no. 227 in Kutná Hora, the old silver-mining town east of Prague. His father, Václav, was a miller there, and his grandfather Mathias Beneš was a handyman in the same house. (Joseph himself later gave his birthday as 22 March 1832, the date on his death certificate.) He trained as a miller like his father, and by the 1850s he was running the mill at Záměl, house no. 26, the mill Libor had bought. There he married Libor's daughter Julia, born in Ústí in 1838. They crossed to America a few months ahead of her parents in 1856.

Joseph kept a handwritten "Family Record" in old script. The original is lost, but other Benesch descendants kept photocopies, and Nancy Prince transcribed one in 2009. In it he wrote that he and Julia sailed in 1856 with their baby, Božena, born at Záměl that July. The ship's list for the Hammonia, which reached New York from Hamburg on 16 September 1856, shows "Jos. Benetsch, 26, miller, baker," his wife Julie, 18, and an infant girl a few weeks old. The family went on to Cedar Rapids, Iowa, where Joseph filed his first citizenship papers in July 1857, with Libor as his witness. Little Božena did not survive that first winter; she died in Cedar Rapids on 17 March 1857. In the 1910 census Julia counted six children born and five living, still remembering her.

They farmed in Burt County, Nebraska, where their daughter Clara was born in April 1862. In the summer of 1864 they loaded the children into a wagon and spent four months on the plains, reaching Denver City on 17 December 1864. They then homesteaded at Piñon, on the Fountain north of Pueblo. Joseph served on the local school board for at least 15 years, and in 1882 he deeded a corner of his homestead to School District No. 4 "to be used for school purposes." Julia died at Piñon on 18 February 1915.

The first year in Colorado was hard too. Joseph wrote that in 1865, on a rented farm near Denver, "the grasshoppers has been destroyed most of our crops," and that fall they moved south to the Fountain.

Life on the Fountain. Joseph's land lay six miles from Libor's, on the east side of Fountain Creek along the old stage road. He built a "grout" house of crushed limestone and river gravel that still stands on Overton Road near the Piñon Bridge. A newspaper writing up the farms along the Fountain judged that "the pretty place of Joseph Bennescher" was a close rival to the best ranch in the valley. When the Denver & Rio Grande railroad came up the far side of the creek in 1871, a flag stop called Piñon Station went in right across from the house. Family legend says Joseph gave land for the school so that Emma, his oldest, wouldn't have to ride the stage to school; it became District No. 4, one of the first in Pueblo County. Families took turns boarding the teacher for $4 a month, and the Benesch house kept the school bell, to ring as an alarm if raiders came. In March 1873 the teacher, Miss Lucy Pastor, was boarding with them when the house burned, taking her clothes and the family's naturalization papers; the young people of the neighborhood took up a collection at a party that weekend and gave her $25 for a new wardrobe. Over the years Joseph sat on a federal jury, joined a Hayes and Wheeler club in the 1876 election, registered a cattle brand, and sold the county a strip of land for the road. There was a Benesch on a Pueblo County school board until the schools were consolidated in 1957.

The Piñon school, probably taken when the "new" building opened about 1907. Nancy Prince says at least six of these children are Benesch descendants, though most aren't identified. The photo is often shared on the "Old Pinon School" Facebook group.

In 1941 a WPA writer recording the history of Piñon noted that the settlement was founded by "a Mr. Schelenger" (Libor), Joseph Benesch and Marion S. Southerland, and that three of Mr. Schelenger's grandchildren, Mrs. Emma Risley, George Benesch and "a Mrs. White", still lived there. Mrs. White was Clara.

Joseph died at his ranch on Friday, 24 August 1917, aged 87. The Pueblo Chieftain called him "the Pueblo county pioneer." At his funeral three young women sang "Abide With Me," "Lead Kindly Light" and "Nearer My God to Thee." The family's story is that the ranch stayed in the family until the Army took the land for the Piñon Canyon Maneuver Site in the early 1980s. We haven't found a record of that yet.

Sources: Pueblo Chieftain, 25–27 Aug 1917; Prince (2013); the 2007 Hrnčiřík parish research.

stories.title: Clara Benesch (1862–1941): she walked out
stories.group: A rebel of 1848, a wagon train to Denver, and a ranch on the Fountain
stories.html:
Clara married Charles Baumeister in Denver on 14 August 1882. On New Year's Day 1892 he beat her to the floor in their Denver home. In February she filed for divorce, describing years of abuse and drunkenness, and asked for sole custody of their eight-year-old son, Chester. It was an unusually brave step for a woman in 1892, and the court file survives at the Colorado State Archives.

On 20 March 1894 she married William John White (1859–1916), a New Yorker by birth. They lost a baby son, Albert, in February 1896. Their son Theodore Roosevelt White was born in Denver on 12 April 1900. William was a Freemason of South Denver Lodge No. 93, and his brother Masons buried him at Riverside Cemetery on 28 May 1916. His funeral notice names his sons Chester, Millard, Theodore and Robert. Clara outlived him by 25 years and died at Piñon in March 1941. She lies beside him at Riverside, under a stone reading simply "WHITE."

Clara (Benesch) White with two of her boys in front of the house, about 1910–15, with a flag hung by the porch. The boys are probably two of Millard (b. 1898), Theodore (b. 1900) and Robert. Which two is still to be worked out.

Sources: Arapahoe Co. District Court case #16809 (1892); Denver funeral notices, May 1916; the family headstone, Riverside Cemetery.

William's own parents are still a mystery. He said his father was born in Ireland in one census and in New York in the next.

stories.title: Don White (1927–2000): a Denver boyhood and a life in the dental supply business
stories.group: A rebel of 1848, a wagon train to Denver, and a ranch on the Fountain
stories.html:
Kristin's grandfather Donald Richard White, who went by Don, was born in Colorado in June 1927. He was the son of Theodore Roosevelt White, a Denver dentist, and Theo Pope, the little girl who had been raised by her McClenathan grandparents. He grew up at 3546 Perry Street in northwest Denver, where the census found the family in 1940 and again in 1950. As boys, Don and his brother Teddy roamed the hills west of Mount Falcon Park near Morrison, around the guest ranch of their great-grandmother "Grandma Spence," Mary McClenathan Pope Spence. In high school Don was president of the Junior Orchestra.

Like his father, Don made his living in dentistry: he worked in the dental supply business, a trade that has carried on in the family since. He and his wife moved often over the years, living in Kansas City, the Dallas–Fort Worth area and Savannah before settling in South Carolina. He died in about 2000. He is buried in Morrison Cemetery, near Grandma Spence, in the foothills where he roamed as a boy.

Sources: 1940 and 1950 censuses, Denver; high school yearbook; family memories. His military service file has been requested.

stories.title: Ora and Mary: a short marriage and a girl raised by her grandparents
stories.group: Warren's father's side, part 2: a Cowpens veteran, a cloth mill on Ten Mile Creek, and a Quaker log house
stories.html:
Ora Isaac Pope was born 5 June 1879 in Greene County, Indiana, the son of Jacob Pope and his second wife Mary Ellis. On 27 November 1902 he married Mary E. McClenathan of Switz City, Indiana, whose family had come from Pennsylvania. They married in Greene County. The marriage lasted less than two years; they divorced in October 1904. Their daughter Theo did not grow up with either parent at first. The 1910 census finds her in Florence, Colorado, in the home of her McClenathan grandparents, while Mary was working in Cañon City as a maid. Theo later took the surname of her stepfather, Spence. Family stories say Ora started out west with the family and then took off partway there. He never made it to Colorado. He stayed in Indiana, worked as a railway foreman, remarried in 1918, and died in Clayton, Hendricks County, in 1938.

Theo (Pope) Spence White, the little girl raised by her McClenathan grandparents, in her high school yearbook portrait, about 1920–22.

Sources: 1902 wedding notice; 1910 census, Florence and Cañon City, Colorado; 1918 Hendricks County marriage application; on file in pope-research and documents/mcclenathan.

stories.title: Jacob Pope: sixteen children, then three more
stories.group: Warren's father's side, part 2: a Cowpens veteran, a cloth mill on Ten Mile Creek, and a Quaker log house
stories.html:
Jacob was born 4 October 1818 in Lawrence County, Indiana, the same year the county was formed. In 1840 he was living next door to the widow Rebecca Pope, very likely his mother. In 1842 he moved his family to Greene County near Switz City, and in 1845 he helped found the Olive Branch Baptist Church, where he stayed a member the rest of his life. His first wife, Matilda Beasley, bore him sixteen children, nine boys and seven girls, before she died in 1863. In 1868 he married Mary Ellis and had three more sons, Ora among them. When Jacob died on 30 June 1892, his obituary noted that all nine of his surviving children were at his bedside. His headstone reads: "Lived as a Christian, as a Christian died."

An uncle-generation tidbit: Jacob's grandfather was probably George Pope Sr. of Lincoln County, Kentucky, whose 1812 will names his "third son, Casper." A Casper Pope married a Rebecca in Clark County, Indiana, in 1811, which would make Casper and Rebecca Jacob's parents. That link is still being proven.

Sources: 1892 obituary and headstone (Find a Grave memorial 12588291); 1840 Lawrence Co. census; 1812 Lincoln Co. KY will, book G p.13; 1811 Clark Co. IN marriage.

A family photograph remembered as one of the sisters of "Grandma Spence," who was Mary McClenathan Pope Spence. The family doesn't know which sister. The card is from the Cashner studio in Sullivan, Indiana. That fits: Mary's father, Thomas McClenathan, died in 1918 just across the Wabash River in Crawford County, Illinois, and Mary married Ora Pope of the next county over, so the McClenathans were living around Sullivan at the turn of the century. Her plain dress looks old-fashioned for its time, so it may be a copy of an earlier picture.

stories.title: From Pabst to Pope: a father's will in Kentucky and a son across the Ohio
stories.group: Warren's father's side, part 2: a Cowpens veteran, a cloth mill on Ten Mile Creek, and a Quaker log house
stories.html:
Also spelled: Pabst, Bobst, Bapst, Papst, Pope; Casper, Gasper, Jasper; Christina, Christiana; Harling, Harlan.

Jacob Pope's family was not always named Pope. A compiled family history of the Pabst, Bobst and Pope families, and Kristin's tree, trace it to Hans Georg Pabst, recorded as born on 23 January 1741 at Fröschen, a village in the Electoral Palatinate (today part of Thaleischweiler-Fröschen). Like thousands of Palatine Germans, the family came to Pennsylvania, and like many of them it followed the frontier south and west. By the time Hans Georg died, he was George Pope Sr. of Lincoln County, Kentucky, one of the three original counties of Kentucky, around Stanford and the old Logan's Fort. The German name had been worn down to an English one, as happened to Pabsts all over the backcountry.

A will that settled scores. George made his will on 1 May 1812, "being in a perfect state of health in body and of sound mind." It is a lively document. He left his wife Christina a bed and furniture of her choosing, "my chest," and four hundred silver dollars. His eldest son, Henry, was dead. George had already given Henry the home plantation of more than 300 acres, and he wrote that Henry's heirs were to be "entirely disinherited and debarred from getting any more of my Estate." Each of the other children was charged with what they had already received. Of "my third son Casper Pope," George wrote that he had advanced him £250 "in land it being the Tract whereon he formerly lived now occupied by Jacob Miller." The will was proved in court on 9 November 1812, so George died that summer or autumn.

Casper crosses the Ohio. That word "formerly" matters: by 1812 Casper had already left Kentucky. On 9 December 1811, "Gasper Pope" married Rebecca in Clark County, across the Ohio River from Louisville, in what was still the Indiana Territory. Indiana did not become a state until 1816. The clerk's spelling of Rebecca's surname is hard to read. Family trees call her Rebecca Harling, and she named a son Harling Pope, which was a common way to pass on a mother's maiden name. The family moved north into the hill country of Lawrence County, where Jacob was born on 4 October 1818, the year the county was formed. Casper died in 1830. In 1840 the census taker in Lawrence County wrote down the widow Rebecca Pope, in her fifties, with four sons at home, and next door to her, Jacob, newly married to Matilda Beasley, with a baby. Rebecca died in Lawrence County on 1 December 1851. Jacob's story is told above.

Still to prove: no single record yet names Jacob as Casper's son. The 1850 census of Lawrence County, or Casper's or Rebecca's estate papers, could settle it.

Sources: will of George Pope Sr., Lincoln Co., KY, Will Book G, pp. 13–14 (FamilySearch images); Clark Co., IN marriage register, vol. A, p. 7; 1840 census, Lawrence Co., IN; "Pape–Pope Family" compiled genealogy (index). Copies in pope-research.

stories.title: Robert Ellis: shot in the heel, wounded at Eutaw Springs, and still asking for his pension at 86
stories.group: Warren's father's side, part 2: a Cowpens veteran, a cloth mill on Ten Mile Creek, and a Quaker log house
stories.html:
Mary Ellis's grandfather was very likely Robert Ellis, a Revolutionary War soldier whose own sworn words survive. In 1838, an old man living in Tennessee, he stood before a court and told his story to get a pension.

He was born 1 February 1760 in Buckingham County, Virginia, and grew up on the South Carolina frontier in Abbeville District. He volunteered every time he served. In the fall of 1780 he marched against the Cherokee and was shot in the heel at Generostee. In January 1781 he fought at Cowpens, the battle where Daniel Morgan's riflemen broke a British army in under an hour. That summer he was at the siege of Ninety Six, where his captain, Joseph Pickens, was killed. In September 1781 he fought at Eutaw Springs, the last major battle in the Carolinas, and took a wound in the left foot. He finished the war as a frontier ranger.

After the war he kept moving: Georgia, then Knox and Campbell Counties in Tennessee (about 30 years there, where his son William was born in 1803), then Greene County, Indiana. His discharge papers were lost when his house burned. He got $30 a year from 1831, and in 1846 Congress added $66 a year for the Eutaw Springs wound. He died in 1849. DAR lists him as patriot A037821.

A family-legend correction: a 1928 newspaper article said Robert was born in Ireland and served in North Carolina regiments. His own sworn testimony says Virginia and South Carolina. Trust Robert.

His son William Ellis (1803–1878) entered 380 acres of government land near Linton, Indiana, in 1835 and farmed there the rest of his life. His daughter Mary appears in his household in 1850 before she married Jacob Pope.

Martha Robertson and the Tennessee frontier. William married Martha Robertson in west Tennessee in 1824, in the Gibson and Dyer County country that had only been opened to settlers a few years before. Martha was born on 13 July 1805 in Tennessee. Kristin's tree gives her parents as Stephen Robertson and Winnie Webb Chitwood, who married on 26 May 1800 at Beaver Creek in Knox County, near Knoxville. Stephen was born about 1775 in southwest Virginia. A family history written down by Fred Robertson in 1956 says he lived around Harrodsburg, Kentucky, until the mid-1790s before moving on to Tennessee; that account gives no sources, so it is family tradition. Winnie was born on 2 June 1784 in Rutherford County, North Carolina. Like the Ellises, the Robertsons ended up in Indiana. Stephen died about November 1837 at Needmore, Brown County, and Winnie in 1840, and both are buried in the Robertson Cemetery there. Martha and William raised a big family on the Linton farm, and one of their sons was named Stephen, after her father, it seems. Martha died at Linton on 11 December 1868 and is buried in Samaria Cemetery. Also spelled: Robertson, Robinson; Winnie, Winifred; Chitwood, Chetwood.

Sources: pension file S26084 (Will Graves's transcription); DAR GRS A037821; 1850 Greene Co. IN census; William Ellis will abstract. The Robert → William link is strongly supported but not yet proven by a record naming them together.

stories.title: The McClenathans and the Vandykes of Amity, Pennsylvania
stories.group: Warren's father's side, part 2: a Cowpens veteran, a cloth mill on Ten Mile Creek, and a Quaker log house
stories.html:
Mary McClenathan's father, Thomas Farland McClenathan (1840–1918), was born in Washington County, Pennsylvania, near the village of Amity. His mother, Irene Vandyke, died on 7 October 1841, barely a year after he was born. She is buried in the Vandyke family row at Lower Ten Mile Cemetery, beside the widow Catharine Vandyke, very likely her mother.

Labeled "John McClenathan and his wife" on a photo shared on MyHeritage. The man's long hair and big bow tie and the woman's lace cap and collar are 1850s to early-1860s styles, and both look about 50. That fits John McClenathan (born 1807) and his second wife Rachel Carter (born 1812), Thomas's stepmother, around 1855–65, so the label is probably right. Thomas's own mother, Irene, died in 1841, before photography reached rural Pennsylvania.

The records of the Amity Presbyterian Church let us watch this family on the page. Catharine is listed as "wife of Martin" in 1818 and as a widow from 1826. Irene was admitted to communion in 1830 as a Vandyke and appears in 1839 as Irene McClenathan.

Thomas's grandfather William McClenathan (1765–1850) was born in Dauphin County and married Mary Coulson, whose parents Samuel and Charity Coulson were early Amwell Township settlers. William and Mary signed for her share of her father's estate in 1812. When William died in 1850, a deed of the next year calls John McClenathan his "son and heir at law."

Sources: Amity Presbyterian session minutes and communicant lists 1818–1839; 1852 Washington Co. death register; 1812 Coulson estate receipt; 1851 administrators' deed; 1918 Illinois death index (names Thomas's parents).

The Coulsons: a family Bible and a Quaker scandal. Mary Coulson's parents' marriage is written in the family Bible in a careful hand: "Samuel Coulson and Charity Death were married Nov. 30, 1779." The death page records Samuel "departed this life" in December 1809 in his 56th year, and Charity on 14 December 1820 in her 63rd year. Her son-in-law William McClenachan took out letters of administration on her estate in January 1821 and ran the notice in the Washington Reporter that fall; the appraisers listed what "Charity Coulson, Widow" had kept back at the appraisal of her husband's estate: a spinning wheel, a bed up in the chamber, a churn, a pepper mill, a smoothing iron, a saddle and a pocketbook.

The Coulsons were Quakers from the Nottingham settlement on the Pennsylvania–Maryland line. A family compilation, "Lineage of the Coulsons," says Samuel's grandfather Thomas Coulson was born in Derbyshire, England, on 15 April 1703, came over as a child with his parents to Germantown, and died on 17 August 1763; he lies in the old Friends' burying ground at West Nottingham, where a small fieldstone cut "T:C 1763" still stands. The Nottingham Monthly Meeting minutes add a very human footnote. On the 10th of the 5th month, 1725, the meeting heard that "Thomas Colson of Notingham hath been Guilty of Commiting ye Sin of fornication" with Martha Wyly, daughter of Allen Wyly of New Garden. Thomas appeared, confessed, and was told to write out a paper condemning it in his own hand. He and Martha married, and their son Samuel (born 1729) married Tamar Allen in 1751 and raised sixteen children, among them our Samuel (1753–1809).

Sources: Coulson family Bible (marriage and death pages, photos in the family's Ancestry tree); Charity Coulson administration bond and notice, 1821; Nottingham MM minutes 1725 (Quaker meeting records); "Lineage of the Coulsons" (compiled, not yet checked against originals).

stories.title: Tamar Allen's Quaker roots: the Bortons of Aynho, the Woolmans of Painswick, and a cousin who spoke against slavery
stories.group: Warren's father's side, part 2: a Cowpens veteran, a cloth mill on Ten Mile Creek, and a Quaker log house
stories.html:
Samuel Coulson's wife, Tamar Allen (1733–1818), came from two of the oldest Quaker families on the Delaware. Her father, John Allen (1708–1758), was a Nottingham Friend, the son of early settlers James Allen and Mary Weaver on the Pennsylvania–Maryland line. Her mother, Esther (Hester) Woolman, was born on 7 September 1706 beside Rancocas Creek in Burlington County, West New Jersey. She was the youngest child of John Woolman and Elizabeth Borton, and through them Tamar's family goes back to two English villages.

From Aynho to Hillsdown. Elizabeth's parents, John Borton and Ann Kinton, married on 12 April 1658 at Aynho, a stone village in Northamptonshire on the Oxfordshire border. The Bortons had been in Aynho for generations, back to a William Borton who died there in 1597. John and Ann joined the Quakers, a movement barely ten years old and outlawed in practice. Joseph Besse's Sufferings of the People Called Quakers (1753) lists John among the Friends taken from their homes by soldiers and jailed in January 1661 for refusing to swear the oath of allegiance. In 1665 he was fined for four weeks' absence from the parish church, and in 1674 his goods were seized for holding meetings. In 1679 their meeting gave John and Ann a certificate saying they had "walked honestly among us," and they sailed with their children to West New Jersey, the new Quaker colony on the Delaware. John paid the Lenape £20 7s for his land and named the farm Hillsdown, on the south side of the Rancocas in what is now Mount Laurel. He died there in July 1687. One of the witnesses to his will was his son-in-law, John Woolman.

From Painswick to the Rancocas. John Woolman (about 1655–1718) is said to have come from Painswick, a Cotswold wool town in Gloucestershire, with his father William, who settled in West Jersey about 1678 and was buried in Burlington County in 1692. On 8 October 1684, under the care of Burlington Monthly Meeting, John married Elizabeth Borton. They farmed beside the Rancocas, then called the Northampton River, and raised a large family there. Both died in 1718 and lie in the Friends' burial ground at Rancocas. Their son Samuel kept the home farm. Esther, the youngest, married John Allen and went west to the Nottingham settlement, where Tamar was born.

Two Allen wills. Tamar's grandfather James Allen was a cooper, a barrel maker, in West Nottingham. When he made his will on 1 April 1733, "sick and weak in body," he left everything to his wife Mary for as long as she stayed a widow, and named their children: Ann Harris, John, Morril, James, William, Isaac, Mary and Nathan. The youngest, Nathan, was to have ten pounds more than the rest. Tamar's father, John Allen, made his own will on 18 February 1758, "weak in body but of a sound and well disposing mind," and it was proved that October. He left plantations in West Nottingham and land in York County to his sons John, Samuel and James, a third of his movable goods to his wife Ester, thirty pounds for his young daughter Patience, and to "my daughter Tamar Coulson one cow as her mother shall choose," along with her share of the rest. Whatever the meeting thought of her marriage, her father had not cut her off. The witnesses added that they heard him say he gave "his mare called Chains" to his son Samuel and a three-year-old bay colt to James.

Married out of meeting. Quakers were strict about marriage. A couple declared their intention twice before the monthly meeting, the meeting checked that both were free to marry, and they married each other in a meeting for worship, with no minister. A Friend who married "out of meeting," before a priest or a magistrate or to someone who was not a Friend, was usually disowned unless they sent the meeting a paper condemning what they had done. Many family genealogies say this is what happened to Tamar when she married Samuel Coulson in 1751. It is a nice echo of her father-in-law's 1725 confession before the same meeting. We have not yet seen the minute itself; it should be in the Nottingham Monthly Meeting minutes for 1751–52.

The cousin who spoke against slavery. Esther's brother Samuel Woolman named his first son John, born on the Rancocas farm on 19 October 1720. That John Woolman, Tamar's first cousin, became one of the first and most persistent voices against slavery in America. As a young clerk in Mount Holly, about 23, he was asked by his employer to write a bill of sale for an enslaved woman. He wrote it, said it troubled him, and after that he refused to write any will or bill of sale that passed people on as property. He became a tailor so that he could travel, and for nearly thirty years he went on foot and horseback among Friends from New England to the Carolinas, sitting with slaveholders and telling them, gently and plainly, that keeping people as property was wrong. When he stayed in a slaveholder's house he paid the enslaved people who waited on him. He published Some Considerations on the Keeping of Negroes in 1754 and a second part in 1762. In 1776 Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, which included Tamar's Nottingham meeting, ruled that Friends who still held slaves would be disowned, and Woolman's long campaign is a large part of why. He wore undyed clothes and refused silver dishes, and he crossed to England in 1772 in steerage, living with the sailors. He caught smallpox and died at York on 7 October 1772. His Journal, published in 1774, has never gone out of print and was chosen for the first volume of the Harvard Classics.

Sources: Burlington Monthly Meeting marriage records (Woolman–Borton, 1684), via Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 2; Amelia Mott Gummere, The Journal and Essays of John Woolman (1922), family records (Hester b. 7 Sep 1706); Stokes, Genealogy of the Stokes Family (1903), p. 11; Aynho parish register (Borton–Kinton marriage, 1658); Besse, Sufferings (1753); Borton certificate of removal, 1679; Freeman C. Mason, The Borton and Mason Families (1908); John Woolman's Journal (1774). Tamar's disownment: family genealogies, minute not yet seen.

stories.title: The Buckinghams: a colonel, a cloth factory, and a DAR line
stories.group: Warren's father's side, part 2: a Cowpens veteran, a cloth mill on Ten Mile Creek, and a Quaker log house
stories.html:
Thomas married Elizabeth Ann Buckingham (1841–1922), and her side of the family is one of the best documented in the whole tree.

Her father, Col. John Buckingham (1797–1882), married Jane Dalrymple, a New Jersey girl. Jane's own parents kept a handwritten family record that notes she was born on a Monday, 15 May 1797. That page survives, and the day of the week checks out.

The same record follows Jane's younger brothers and sisters, and it is full of quiet losses: her brother Joseph "died September the 6th 1829 aged 20 years ... a young man"; and her youngest brother William Andrew, born on a Thursday, 22 February 1816, "died November 26th 1834, a young man aged 18 years 9 months 4 days." Jane's mother Esther died on 19 December 1837, and the Washington Examiner gave her age exactly: 64 years and 7 months.

Jane and John Buckingham also raised one of the family's orphans. Her nephew George Washington Dalrymple wrote a short note late in life: "my Father was James Dalrymple, my mother was Lydia Ann Fowler who died when I was 3 months old. Then John Buckingham and his wife who was my Father's sister took me and kept me till I enlisted in the Civil War." He was born on 22 February 1848 in Washington County, went off to the war as a teenager, and afterwards "has been in the West since the Civil War." His papers include a 1909 note from the Bank of Ephrata in Washington State and an 1899 Iowa newspaper clipping about welcoming home soldiers.

John's father, Isaac Buckingham (1777–1833), ran the "Ten-Mile factory," a cloth mill on Ten Mile Creek. In 1822 he won $10 for the best piece of domestic cloth from the county agricultural society, and he ran ads for the factory in the Washington Reporter for years. After he died, his estate paid off his newspaper subscription going back to 1816. The receipt, signed in 1835, says it was paid by "Col. John Buckingham, one of the administrators." Isaac married Hannah Heaton, whose father Isaac Heaton was himself a patriot (DAR A054036).

Isaac's father, John Buckingham (1741–1794), was a private and company clerk in the Washington County militia during the Revolution. His headstone says he died "aged 53 years and 20 days" and calls him one of the first settlers. He is DAR patriot A016510, and DAR already lists Isaac as his proven child. That makes this the easiest DAR line in the family.

Sources: Dalrymple family record; Isaac Buckingham estate receipt, 11 May 1835; Crumrine, History of Washington County (1882), pp. 473 and 973 (free on archive.org); DAR card A016510; headstones on Find a Grave.

stories.title: The Bowens and the Moons: from Penn's colony to the Virginia frontier
stories.group: Warren's father's side, part 2: a Cowpens veteran, a cloth mill on Ten Mile Creek, and a Quaker log house
stories.html:
Hannah Heaton's mother was Hannah Bowen (1741–1827), born at Apple Pie Ridge near Winchester, Virginia, in the Quaker settlement around Hopewell Meeting. Her mother's father was Simon Moon. When Simon wrote his will in 1748, he named his son-in-law Henry Bowen. Simon had married Leaury Humphrey at Christ Church, Philadelphia, on 27 September 1721. That was Ben Franklin's church, a slightly surprising choice for a Quaker family. Simon and his daughter Lauretha now lie under plain fieldstones at Hopewell.

Simon's grandfather James Moon Sr. married Joan Burgess near Bristol, England, and came to Pennsylvania in 1682, the year William Penn founded the colony. By 1688 he owned 125 acres in Falls Township, Bucks County, near the Quaker village of Fallsington. His will is remembered for one hard line: he left his "eldest son James" just one shilling. That was a common way to make sure a child couldn't later claim he'd been forgotten; James Jr. had likely been provided for already. Joan died on 2 December 1739. Both are buried in the old Friends burial ground at Fallsington in unmarked graves, as Quakers then preferred.

The Moon house. In 1722 a fire destroyed James Moon's home, and the local Friends raised money to help the family. The Moon log house that still stands in Fallsington today sits on land that belonged to Samuel Burgess, Joan's father. It is first documented in 1760 and was lived in by Samuel Moon, a nephew, in 1769. So it is a family house, though probably not the one James Sr. himself lived in. It has three connected sections, each with its own door, corner fireplaces, a bread oven, and a well out back. The two sycamores in front of it appear on a 1760 map of the village. It is part of Historic Fallsington and worth a visit.

The Moon log house in Fallsington, Pennsylvania.

Sources: Simon Moon will, 1748; Christ Church marriage register, 1721; James Moon Sr. will transcription; Fallsington meeting records; photos sent by Kristin and saved in documents/bowen-moon. The Simon → James Jr. link is still Probable; James Jr.'s 1755 Bucks County probate would settle it.

stories.title: "Carl York": the grandfather who wasn't a York
stories.group: Warren's mother's side: a man with two names, a bear hunt in Arizona, and a baby bound out at one year old
stories.html:
Warren's mother grew up hearing that her father, Carl York, had been killed as a bystander in a robbery. The truth turned up in the Rocky Mountain News of 10 May 1935, under the headline "Denver Woman's Husband Shot, Identified as Thief."

"Carl York," very likely Harvey Wade, in a photo-booth portrait from the early 1930s, from the family's own collection.

Carl York, 22, a barber by trade, had been shot five times by Los Angeles police at his apartment on 9 May 1935. He had been working as an undercover informant for one detective, and a second team of officers, staking out the same apartment, didn't know it. They said he reached for his pocket. That night nine parking-lot attendants identified him as one of the gunmen who had been robbing them. He died two days later, and a coroner's jury called it justifiable. The paper said his wife, Mildred York, lived in Denver, and that their two-year-old daughter was staying with Mildred's parents in Greeley.

The bigger surprise was who Carl really was. He told the world he came from Canton, Ohio, but no York family of that kind existed there. His death certificate gives his parents as William and Lou, his birthplace as Canton, and a December birthday. DNA settled the rest: Kristin's family matches strongly with the descendants of Will and Lou Wade of Canton, Georgia, and with no Yorks at all. Their eldest son, Harvey Wade, born about December 1912, vanishes from the records after 1930. And his daughter's middle name, Jewel, matches Harvey's sister Jewel Wade.

How sure: Harvey as Will and Lou's son is proven by the 1920 and 1930 censuses. Harvey = Carl York is strongly supported by DNA and the 1935 records, but not yet proven by a single document.

Sources: Rocky Mountain News, 10 May 1935 (free, Colorado Historic Newspapers); Los Angeles death certificate no. 6501; 1920 and 1930 censuses; DNA matches.

stories.title: The Wades: miners in the hills of the first American gold rush
stories.group: Warren's mother's side: a man with two names, a bear hunt in Arizona, and a baby bound out at one year old
stories.html:
Harvey's father, Will R. Wade (1888–1929), was a miner who died of pneumonia at 40 in the town of White, Bartow County, Georgia. His death certificate names his parents as Bill Wade and Kizzy Trammel. Will had married Lou Newton in Cherokee County in 1909, when she was about 14. The family lost a three-month-old daughter, George Ida Mae, in Canton in 1926.

Bill Wade was born in 1865 in Auraria, Lumpkin County, and Kizzie's father Peter Newell Trammell died there in 1907. Auraria was the boom town of the Georgia Gold Rush of 1829, the first major gold rush in the United States. It emptied out when miners left for California and Colorado. Some Auraria men even named a camp in Colorado after it, the settlement that became part of Denver. So Warren's Georgia side and his Colorado side were tied together by gold long before the family knew it.

The grandparents in gold country. Both sides of the family were in Auraria almost from the start. Bill Wade's father, Charles Wade, was born about 1813 in South Carolina and was living in the Auraria district in 1850, 1860 and 1880. On 5 August 1854 he married Hannah Davis, about 19, also South Carolina-born. Kizzie's father, Peter Trammell, was born in Georgia in 1820, the son of James Trammell, who died in Lumpkin County in 1848. In 1840 Peter was living in Walker County, in the far northwest of Georgia, on land the Cherokee had been forced out of only two years before, on the Trail of Tears. That same gold-and-land rush opened Lumpkin County. Peter's wife, Mary Jane Whitener, was born at Auraria on 1 June 1838, the year the U.S. Mint opened in nearby Dahlonega to coin the local gold. Her parents, Jacob Whitener of North Carolina and Keziah Landrum, born in 1808 in Lincoln County, North Carolina, had married in Lumpkin County in 1836. Keziah died at Auraria in January 1866, and eight years later her granddaughter was named Hannah Keziah after her. Peter and Mary Jane married at the end of the Civil War and stayed in Auraria the rest of their lives; Peter died there in 1907 and Mary Jane in 1910. Bill and Kizzie later moved west to Cherokee and Bartow counties, where Bill died at Cartersville in 1937 and Kizzie in 1949. Also spelled: Trammell, Trammel; Whitener, Whitner; Keziah, Kizzie, Kissie.

Sources: 1929 Georgia death certificate (Will R. Wade); 1909 Cherokee Co. marriage; Georgia Virtual Vault, 1926 death of George Ida Mae Wade; 1900 census.

stories.title: Arthur Hoover: a bear hunt, a worn-out safety, and a man who took ten years off his age
stories.group: Warren's mother's side: a man with two names, a bear hunt in Arizona, and a baby bound out at one year old
stories.html:
Mildred's father, Arthur J. Hoover, married Laura Jane Smith at her parents' home in La Salle, Colorado, on 16 March 1910. The Greeley Tribune described the wedding: an arch of smilax and wedding bells between the parlors, a bride in white with bride's roses, and the wedding march from Tannhäuser played on the violin. Arthur was a machinery man who had worked for the Colorado & Southern railroad, on the Milton reservoir job, and for Laura's father.

Arthur and Laura's daughter Mildred Eva Hoover, born 20 December 1910, in a long white eyelet dress, probably about 1911–12. The card is stamped by the Roberts studio.

Nine years later the family was in Thatcher, Arizona, where Arthur worked at a lumber mill in the Graham Mountains. On Sunday, 12 October 1919, he and two other men were walking back from a bear hunt and stopped to rest. An old rifle whose safety had worn down went off, and the bullet shattered his left leg. His companions carried him eight miles down the mountain on a stretcher to a waiting car. Infection set in, the leg was amputated, and he died at the Safford hospital a few days later. He was 39 by the newspaper's count and left a wife and five children. Mildred was eight.

Probably not 39. The evidence suggests Arthur was really Archibald "Arch" J. Hoover, born about 1871 in Rockingham County, Virginia, the only child of Hiram Hoover and Eva Ritchie. Arch had farmed in Illinois, was divorced there in 1909, and seems to have come west and started over with a younger age. Hiram's 1930 obituary names his son "Archie James." This is strongly supported but not yet proven.

A Hiram Hoover family photo posted on Find a Grave. The people in it are not identified in a record.

Sources: Greeley Tribune, 17 March 1910 (free); Graham Guardian, Safford, 17 Oct 1919; 1880 and 1900 censuses; 1909 Monmouth, IL divorce notice; Hiram Hoover's 1930 obituary.

stories.title: The Ritchies and Fulks of Brock's Gap, Virginia
stories.group: Warren's mother's side: a man with two names, a bear hunt in Arizona, and a baby bound out at one year old
stories.html:
Eva Ritchie (1855–1902) was born in the Shenandoah Valley's Rockingham County, and her 1855 birth register entry names her parents, Philip Ritchie and Eve Fulk. She married Hiram Hoover in 1870 and is buried at Singers Glen.

Eve Fulk's father, Daniel Fulk, owned a piece of mountain land called the "Bible Tract." After he died in 1857, all seven of his other heirs sold their shares of it to Philip Ritchie, Eve's husband, between 1859 and 1862. That is how we know Eve was Daniel's daughter. A family memorial stone for the Fulks still stands in the Fawley-Fulk cemetery. This was German-speaking Mennonite and Brethren country, and Hiram's own parents, Abraham Hoover and Hannah Roadcap, are buried at Salem Mennonite.

One generation further back. The 1857 Rockingham death register, the first year the county kept one, gives both of Eva's grandfathers' families. Philip Ritchie's mother, Margaret Winters, died at Brock's Gap on 20 March 1857, aged 77; she had married Philip Ritchie Sr. on 12 January 1801, and their son Adam was christened that November at the German Reformed Church in Loudoun County. That September, Daniel Fulk died at Brock's Gap of bilious fever, aged 65, and the register names his parents as John and Eve Fulk.

One more Hoover generation. Abraham and Hannah's marriage bond was dated 5 June 1837, and their son Hiram's 1870 marriage register names them as his parents. Going back another step, the Rockingham County marriage returns for 1811 record Jacob Hoover marrying Elizabeth Lamb (Lahm) on 12 September 1811. Abraham was born eleven months later, in August 1812. In the Hoover family cemetery survey, Elizabeth (born 21 March 1784) is noted as the "mother of David and Abraham Hoover." No record yet names Abraham's parents outright, so Jacob and Elizabeth are probable rather than proven.

Sources: Rockingham Co. birth register, 1855; 1870 marriage register; 1831 marriage bond index; Fulk heirs' deeds 1859–62; headstone photos in hoover-research.

stories.title: The Smiths of Varick
stories.group: Warren's mother's side: a man with two names, a bear hunt in Arizona, and a baby bound out at one year old
stories.html:
Laura Jane Smith's father, Charles Augustus Smith, was born about 1862 in Waterloo, New York, and moved west to Hampton, Nebraska, and then Colorado. His father, Thomas Jefferson Smith (1824–1901), and grandparents Anthony and Catharine Smith lived in Varick, Seneca County, New York, in the Finger Lakes.

Thomas Jefferson Smith married Nancy Elizabeth Fullner, who was born about 1828 in New York. Like their son Charles, they went west, and Nancy died in 1899 at Hampton, Nebraska, on the open prairie a long way from the Finger Lakes. Also spelled: Fullner, Fulner, Follner.

The family has always handed down that the Smiths had Native American ancestry, and it is a heritage the family still holds close. Their corner of New York was a lively place in those years: Seneca County hosted the 1848 Women's Rights Convention at Seneca Falls, and it had stops on the Underground Railroad.

A French-Canadian fur trapper? Another story came down through Grandma's great-aunts: that Anthony Smith's father was a French-Canadian fur trapper. It sits easily beside the Native American tradition, because French traders and trappers often married into Native families, and in the 1790s the fur trade still ran through New York and Pennsylvania along the rivers to the Great Lakes. No record found so far names Anthony's father. The censuses say Anthony was born in Pennsylvania about 1795–97, and "Smith" can hide another name: the French Lefebvre and Forgeron both mean smith. For now this is a family story waiting for its proof.

Sources: 1820 Fayette census; Anthony Smith's deed (1872); family tradition.

stories.title: Mary Catherine Lehman: the baby who was bound out
stories.group: Warren's mother's side: a man with two names, a bear hunt in Arizona, and a baby bound out at one year old
stories.html:
Charles Smith's wife, Mary Catherine Lehman (1868–1953), was raised by George Henry Lehman, a Swiss immigrant, and his wife Sophronia, who was Thomas Jefferson Smith's sister. But she wasn't their birth daughter. Papers kept by Kristin's grandmother show she was indentured at about one year old, around 1869. In that era, an infant was usually bound out by the county's Superintendent of the Poor or by an orphan asylum, often when a mother was unmarried, poor or had died. The papers may give her birth name as "Emma Bartle," but that's still unconfirmed. Who her real parents were is one of the open mysteries in the tree, and the indenture itself is the best clue.

Sources: indenture papers (family collection, not yet photographed); 1870 census, Waterloo, NY; Lehman family records.

stories.title: George and Joseph Lehman: two brothers in the 148th New York
stories.group: Warren's mother's side: a man with two names, a bear hunt in Arizona, and a baby bound out at one year old
stories.html:
Mary Catherine Lehman's foster father, George Henry Lehman, was a 20-year-old Swiss-born farm boy in Waterloo, New York, when Lincoln called for 300,000 more volunteers in 1862. On 28 August 1862 he and Joseph Lehman, his 19-year-old brother, enlisted together at Waterloo and were mustered in as privates in Company H of the 148th New York, the Seneca County regiment. The 148th spent 1863 on guard duty in the Virginia tidewater, then went into the 1864 campaign against Richmond.

At Cold Harbor, on 3 June 1864, Grant threw his army at entrenched Confederate lines in one of the bloodiest mornings of the war. Joseph Lehman was killed in action that day.

By then the 148th belonged to the XVIII Corps of General Butler's Army of the James. It had already lost 78 men in the May fighting below Richmond before being shipped up the York River to join Grant. The assault at Cold Harbor began at about 4:30 in the morning; most of the attacking lines were shot to pieces within minutes, and survivors dug in with bayonets and tin cups a few dozen yards from the Confederate works. Over the twelve days at Cold Harbor the 148th lost 124 men killed, wounded or missing. Joseph was 21.

George survived, and the regiment marched straight on to Petersburg, where in the first assaults of 15–18 June 1864 it lost another 116 men. On 29 September 1864 it helped storm Fort Harrison at Chaffin's Farm, one of the few Union breakthroughs on the Richmond lines; three men of the 148th won the Medal of Honor that day, two of them mortally wounded.

George kept going. On 27 October 1864, at Second Fair Oaks, the regiment charged across a wide-open field at Confederate works outside Richmond and got within about 150 yards before the line broke under fire from the front and both flanks. George was captured in action. He spent the winter as a prisoner, and men taken there were usually held at Salisbury, North Carolina. He was paroled on 2 April 1865 at North East Bridge, a week before Appomattox, and discharged at Rochester on 20 July 1865. He came home to Waterloo, married Sophronia Smith, and later took in a one-year-old girl who became Mary Catherine Lehman.

The regiment's own report of that afternoon is grim reading: of the men who went in, 1 was killed, 19 wounded and 64 missing, 84 in all, and the officer who led the charge, Capt. E. Darwin Gage, was among those lost. Most of the "missing" were men like George who were pinned down in the open and swept up by the Confederates when the line fell back. By the end of the war the 148th had lost 267 men, and 24 of its enlisted men died as prisoners, so George was lucky to come home at all. The regiment was mustered out at Richmond on 22 June 1865.

Sources for the regimental details: Frederick Phisterer, New York in the War of the Rebellion (1912), 148th Infantry; Official Records ser. I vol. 42 pt. 1, report of the 148th NY on the 27 Oct 1864 action; Fox, Regimental Losses (1889).

Source: New York Adjutant-General's roster of the 148th NY Infantry (PDF, free), entries for George and Joseph Lehman; found by Kristin. Kristin confirmed Joseph was George's brother.

stories.title: Henry Koetter: off the boat and into the Union army
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Heinrich Friedrich "Henry" Koetter was born in 1838 in the Schaumburg area of northern Germany; a village history booklet for Auhagen and Düdinghausen has come down in the family. He came to St. Louis, a city where nearly a third of the people were German-born, and when the Civil War broke out he joined the Union side. His pension card shows service in Company D, 5th Missouri Infantry, and Company E of the 5th U.S. Reserve Corps. These German regiments, raised in a slave state, helped keep Missouri in the Union in 1861, in the weeks after the capture of Camp Jackson that May.

What his two units did in the summer of 1861. Both were short-term German outfits raised in a hurry in St. Louis.

  • The 5th Missouri (three-month regiment), under Col. Charles E. Salomon, was the first regiment mustered in after Camp Jackson. It marched to southwest Missouri with Franz Sigel and fought at Carthage on 5 July 1861, a running fight in which Sigel's 1,100 Germans fell back for miles in good order before a Missouri State Guard force several times their size. On 10 August 1861 it was in Sigel's column at Wilson's Creek, the first big battle west of the Mississippi, where Sigel's flank attack was routed and General Nathaniel Lyon was killed. The regiment was mustered out by the end of August. (We still need Henry's service record to be sure he was in this three-month regiment and not a later 5th Missouri.)
  • The 5th U.S. Reserve Corps was a home-guard regiment of St. Louis Germans organized on 11 May 1861, the day after Camp Jackson. On its first march through the city, a hostile crowd at Fifth and Market streets jeered and fired on the column; the soldiers fired back and several people were killed, the second deadly street clash in St. Louis in two days. Detachments later served at Lexington (9 July) and Blue Mills Landing (24 July) in western Missouri before the regiment was mustered out on 31 August 1861.

Called out again in 1864. Henry served one more time. A Missouri militia service card shows Sergeant Henry Koetter, Company E, 13th Regiment, Enrolled Missouri Militia (Captain Heidemann), enrolled at St. Louis in 1864. He was ordered into active service on 25 September 1864 and relieved on 31 October 1864. Those are the weeks of Confederate General Sterling Price's raid into Missouri, when the militia of St. Louis was called out because the city itself seemed to be in danger.

Source: Missouri militia service card, Henry Koetter, 13th Regt. E.M.M. (FamilySearch, "Missouri, Miscellaneous" image 1841). Saved in documents/koetter/.

Sources: Missouri Digital Heritage Soldiers' Records; Dyer, Compendium of the War of the Rebellion (1908); Official Records ser. I vol. 3. Henry's service record and pension file (NARA) would confirm which companies he was with on which dates.

In 1871 Henry married Lisette Zuroweste, whose father Rudolph had come over from Bremen to New Orleans in 1852, probably from the village of Sögeln near Bramsche. Henry filed for an invalid's pension in 1890, died on 7 January 1901, and Lisette filed as his widow two weeks later. They share a headstone at Friedens Cemetery in St. Louis.

Their son Fred H. Koetter (1872–1934) married Emma Pauline Blum and lived at 2564 Natural Bridge Avenue. Their son Fred Henry Koetter (1900–1978), Vernon's father, registered for the World War I draft at 18 from that same address.

Emma's secret. Nobody in the family knew that Emma had been adopted until Kristin found the will of Caroline Niemeier. In the 1880 census Emma appears as "Emma Niemeier," about 6, a daughter in the St. Louis household of Henry and Caroline Niemeier, with brothers and a sister Henry, Caroline and William. But Caroline's will calls her "my adopted daughter" and "the daughter of Henry Blum." So the Blum name Emma married under was her birth name. Who her birth mother was, and how she came to the Niemeiers, are still open questions. In Missouri before 1917, adoptions were made by deed and filed with the Recorder of Deeds, so a St. Louis deed from the late 1870s may hold the answer.

Sources: 1880 census, St. Louis; will of Caroline Niemeier (found by Kristin); Emma Koetter's 1954 death certificate.

Sources: pension index card (free, FamilySearch); 1871 marriage; 1880 and 1900 censuses; 1852 passenger index; death certificates 1912, 1934, 1954; WWI draft card.

stories.title: The zur Oevestes of Bramsche: a name that came with the farm
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Also spelled: zur Oeveste, Zur Oveste, Zurwoeste, Zuroweste, Zuröweste, Zurweste; Müller, Mueller, Möller; Lisette, Lizzette, Elisabeth.

Henry Koetter's wife Lisette came from Bramsche, a small Lutheran town just north of Osnabrück, in what was then the Kingdom of Hanover. Bramsche was a weaving town, known for its cloth makers. A few miles east, in the Bramsche district of Kalkriese, archaeologists in the late 1980s found the place where Germanic tribes destroyed three Roman legions under Varus in the year 9 AD, the battle that kept Rome out of northern Germany. Lisette's family lived at Sögeln, a village on the edge of the town.

A name that came with the farm. In this part of Germany a family often took its surname from the farm it lived on, and a woman who married onto a farm took its name too. The church book shows it plainly: it calls Lisette's mother "Kathr. Maria zur Oeveste, alias Müller," the farm name first and her birth name beside it.

stories.title: Hermann Rudolph zur Oeveste (1799–before 1869) and Catharina: from Bramsche to St. Louis
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Rudolph and Catharina. Hermann Rudolph zur Oeveste was born on 24 November 1799, the son of Hermann Heinrich zur Oeveste and Margaretha Buchtmann. On 18 December 1829, in the Bramsche church, he married Catharina Marie Müller, born on Christmas Day 1807 or 1808, the daughter of Bernd Müller and Catharina Marie Beiß. On that page the clerk put two couples' parents in the wrong columns, then wrote a note in the margin to set it right, which is how we know whose parents are whose. Their children included Regina, Hermann Rudolph (born 1841), Heinrich, Rudolph, and Catharina Lisette Adelheid, born on 10 September 1848 and baptized at Bramsche on 8 October.

Across the ocean, 1852. Rudolph, a farmer of about 52, sailed from Bremen and landed at New Orleans on 23 October 1852. The passenger index gives his home as "Sogelm," a misreading of Sögeln. Lisette, who was four, seems to have come with him. Like most Germans who landed at New Orleans, they would have gone on by steamboat to St. Louis. They may not have been the first of the family there: a note on Catharina's memorial says Regina married in St. Louis in March 1848, and if that is right, she had gone ahead, and may be the reason they chose the city.

A widow on North 12th Street. Rudolph died in St. Louis before 1869. The 1875 city directory lists Kathrina Zurowaste, widow of Rudolph, at 2507 North 12th Street, with her son Rudolph, a cooper, boarding with her. Her son Henry was a cooper too, a few blocks away, and son Herman was in business as McDonald & Zurowaste. Coopers made barrels, and in a brewing city like St. Louis, with dozens of German breweries, barrels were always wanted. Catharina died on 3 November 1884 at 1952 North Broadway, aged 76 years, 10 months and 9 days. The German newspaper Westliche Post printed her death notice the next day, naming her children Hermann, Heinrich, Rudolph, Regina and Lisette, and her sister Maria Heilage, also born Müller. She is buried at Gatewood Gardens Cemetery (once called New Picker's).

Lisette married Henry Koetter in 1871. She died a widow on 7 August 1912 at 913 Clinton Street, of pneumonia, and her death certificate names her parents as "Rud. Zurweste" and "Katherine Mueller."

Sources: Bramsche Lutheran registers (marriage 1829, baptisms 1841 and 1848), images and FamilySearch indexes; New Orleans arrival index, 23 Oct 1852; St. Louis city directory, 1875; Westliche Post, 4 Nov 1884, via Find a Grave 275746413; Lizzette Koetter's 1912 death certificate. Copies in documents/koetter/zuroweste-2026-11-21.

stories.title: Melvin Koetter (born 1924) in World War II
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Two Koetter men went into uniform in World War II: Donna's uncle Melvin, a teenager, and his uncle Oliver, a married man in his late thirties.

Melvin Koetter was born in St. Louis on 1 November 1924, the older brother of Donna's father, Vernon. In 1935 and 1940 the census found the family at 7101 Lexington in Normandy Township, just northwest of the city line. Melvin turned 17 a month before Pearl Harbor. A family portrait shows him in the uniform of the Army Air Forces, the branch that grew from about 150,000 men in 1941 to some 2.4 million by 1944, as the country built the bomber fleets that flew over Germany and Japan. Records name him both Melvin Robards Koetter, after his mother's family, and Melvin Jean Koetter, so he seems to have carried two middle names. His parents' death notices in 1978 and 1979 name him as their son. He died at Wright City, Missouri, on 24 February 2021, aged 96.

stories.title: Oliver W. Koetter (1906–1973): drafted at 37
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html: Oliver William Koetter, Melvin's uncle, was born in St. Louis on 26 July 1906. He was 37 and married when the Army took him on 28 July 1943, as the draft reached deeper into older men and husbands. His serial number, 37 620 652, marks him as a draftee from the 7th Service Command, which took in Missouri. He served from 19 August 1943 until 10 October 1945, two months after the war ended. He lived on Shreve Avenue in north St. Louis and died in July 1973.

stories.title: Mildred Ann Koetter (1912–1953): a sister in Seattle
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Mildred Ann Koetter, Oliver's younger sister, was born in St. Louis on 22 June 1912. She is the family's mystery. She died far from home, in Seattle, on 17 April 1953, aged 40. We don't yet know what took her west. Seattle boomed during the war with Boeing's bomber plants and the shipyards, and many Midwestern women went there for work, but for Mildred that is only a guess.

Sources: 1935 and 1940 censuses; WWII Army enlistment record and VA BIRLS file for Oliver W. Koetter; death notices of Fred H. Koetter (May 1978) and Eleanor W. Koetter (Aug 1979); family photographs. To find: Melvin's service number (BIRLS or enlistment record) to order his file; Mildred's 1953 Washington death certificate (free on the Washington State Digital Archives), which would give her address, occupation and cause of death.

stories.title: Vernon Koetter (1927–2018): the Navy, a season in Alaska, and McDonnell Douglas
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Vernon Marion Koetter was born in St. Louis on 18 February 1927, the son of Fred Henry Koetter and Eleanor Robards. He grew up at 7101 Lexington in Normandy, just outside the city line, with his older brother Melvin. When he registered for the draft at 18, in 1945, he was a student at Drury College in Springfield. He went into the Navy as the war was ending and served as a Seaman First Class.

After the war Vern made his way to Alaska, still a territory then, and spent a season working in the logging camps there. It stayed one of his fondest memories.

Vern spent his career as an accountant with McDonnell Douglas, formed in 1967 when McDonnell Aircraft of St. Louis merged with Douglas Aircraft of southern California. He moved back and forth between the company's California and Missouri plants, which is why the family was living in Downey, California, in 1961. When he retired, he and Jean moved to their farm near Montgomery City, Missouri. Vern died on 10 June 2018, aged 91, and is buried at Bethel Methodist Cemetery near the farm. Through his mother he is the link to the Robards line, back to the Revolutionary sergeant William Robards.

Sources: WWII draft card (1945); Navy muster roll; 1930, 1935 and 1940 censuses; parents' death notices (1978, 1979); Elsa Dittrich's 1961 death certificate; family memories.

stories.title: William Robards Jr.: a Revolutionary sergeant
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Vernon's mother, Eleanor Robards (1901–1979), came from a family whose papers go back to colonial Virginia.

William Robards Jr. served from Goochland County, Virginia, during the Revolution as an orderly, a commissary and finally a sergeant. He was at the burning of Richmond by Benedict Arnold's troops in 1781 and at the Battle of Camden in South Carolina. Two of his brothers were officers in the same companies. He married Elizabeth Lewis in Goochland in 1780 or 1781 and moved to Jessamine County, Kentucky. When she applied for a widow's pension at 78, she listed their children, including Otho Robards, born February 23, 1794. His father, William Robards Sr., is DAR patriot A096624 for supplying the army.

stories.title: Otho Singleton Robards (1794–1857): a sheriff and a house called Thornwood
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Otho Singleton Robards (1794–1857) became sheriff of Jessamine County, a Presbyterian deacon, and a Whig. In 1847 he built Thornwood, a house three miles northwest of Nicholasville that still appears in county historic-homes booklets. Like many prosperous Kentuckians of his day, he was also a large slaveholder, and that is part of the family's story too. He married Cassa Pitts, a young widow; she outlived him by 34 years and died in 1891 at 89.

The cousin in Congress. Look closely at the names: our ancestor was Otho Singleton Robards, and he had a cousin named Otho Robards Singleton (1814–1889). He was born near Nicholasville, the son of Lewis Singleton, a hemp manufacturer. William Robards Jr.'s 1823 will names a daughter "Rebecca Singleton," and his mother was Otho's sister Rebecca, which made him Otho's nephew and Younger Pitts Robards's first cousin. He studied law at Transylvania University, moved to Canton, Mississippi, and served in the state legislature. He went on to serve many terms in the U.S. House: 1853–55, 1857 until he walked out when Mississippi seceded in January 1861, and again from 1875 to 1887. In between he was a Confederate infantry captain and then a member of both Confederate Congresses, where he chaired the Committee on Indian Affairs. He died in Washington, D.C., in 1889 and is buried at Canton.

Sources: Wikipedia: Otho R. Singleton, drawing on the Biographical Directory of the U.S. Congress (House history entry); William Robards Jr.'s 1823 will. His mother identified by Kristin.

Their son Younger Pitts Robards (1833–1899) moved to Missouri, and his son George Caldwell Robards (1869–1933) was Eleanor's father.

Labeled "Younger Pitts Robards" on MyHeritage. But the stand-up collar, puffed tie and swept-up hair are 1890s styles, and this man looks about 25 to 30. Younger was born in 1833 and would have been about 60 then. So it is more likely his son George Caldwell Robards (born 1869), Eleanor's father, in the mid-1890s.

Sources: widow's pension W.8562 (1909 Bureau of Pensions summary); William Robards Jr.'s 1823 will; Thornwood house history; J. H. Robards, History and Genealogy of the Robards Family (about 1906); 1880 census, Callaway Co., MO.

stories.title: John Robards (died 1755): a lot at the falls of the James
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
The Robards papers go back three generations before Otho, and every link from Otho up to his great-grandfather John is now backed by a will or a pension.

John Robards (died 1755) farmed in Goochland County, Virginia, on the James River above modern Richmond. His will, written on 5 December 1754, leaves his wife Sarah the use of part of the house and land, and leaves the plantation to his only named son, William. It also gives his grandsons John and William a horse, a saddle and a town lot in Westham, a little river town at the falls of the James. That grandson William is our William Robards Jr., the Revolutionary sergeant.
