stories.title: William Robards Sr. (about 1729–1783): 6,000 acres in Kentucky, and Andrew Jackson's rival
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
William Robards Sr. (about 1729–1783) was a county leader. He served as a militia lieutenant in the French and Indian War and sat on Goochland's Committee of Safety in 1775, the local body that ran the county for the patriots as royal government collapsed. DAR lists him as patriot A096624. He married twice. His first wife, whose name is still unknown, was the mother of John, William Jr., James and Jane. His second wife, Elizabeth Lewis, daughter of Joseph Lewis, bore seven more. His will of 16 November 1783 shows a family about to move west: it passes a Treasury warrant for 6,000 acres to his sons, plus Kentucky land on the frontier. He died within a month. His widow and younger children went on to Cane Run in Mercer County, Kentucky, near Harrodsburg, and later built a stone house by a spring there.

The half-uncle in the history books. William Jr.'s half-brother Capt. Lewis Robards (1758–1814), a fellow Revolutionary veteran, married a 17-year-old named Rachel Donelson at Harrodsburg on 1 March 1785. The marriage was unhappy. Rachel went back to her family near Nashville, where she met a young lawyer named Andrew Jackson. She and Jackson married believing Lewis had gotten a divorce, but the divorce wasn't final until 1793, and they had to marry again in 1794. Nearly forty years later, in the 1828 presidential election, Jackson's opponents made Rachel's "bigamy" a national scandal. She died that December, just before Jackson took office, and he always blamed his enemies for it. Lewis remarried and had ten children with Hannah Winn. His brother George and mother Elizabeth appear in our 1805 will.

The half-aunt who married a hero of the Revolution. Lewis's sister Sally Robards married Jack Jouett. Jouett is famous for his ride of June 1781: he galloped about 40 miles through the night over back roads to warn Thomas Jefferson and the Virginia legislature that British cavalry under Banastre Tarleton was coming to capture them. Jefferson escaped Monticello with minutes to spare. Jack and Sally settled in Kentucky, and their son Matthew Harris Jouett became Kentucky's best-known portrait painter; he painted Lafayette. Elizabeth Robards's 1805 will mentions a colt she had given to a George Jouett.

The uncle on Aaron Burr's jury panel. William Robards Jr.'s wife, Elizabeth Lewis, was the daughter of William Lewis and Hannah Underwood of Goochland. Hannah's brother was very likely Thomas Underwood, a Goochland planter and merchant of the "Lickinhole" plantation. Before the Revolution he ran up a debt of more than £2,000 to the London merchants John Norton & Sons, and William Lewis stood as one of his securities. In 1790 Thomas wrote that he would move to Kentucky once his affairs were settled. In September 1807, when Aaron Burr was tried in Richmond, "Thomas Underwood, sen." was called in the jury pool. Burr himself challenged him, arguing that Underwood already had an unfavorable opinion of him, and Underwood agreed that he did, so he was excused. So Burr turns up in this family too.

Sources: Virginia Argus (Richmond), 9 Sep 1807, p. 2, "Trial of Aaron Burr" (found by Kristin); John Norton & Sons papers, Colonial Williamsburg; 1789 Goochland mortgage. Thomas as Hannah's brother is likely but not yet proven.

The family also owned slaves. The Robards wills name dozens of enslaved people, from Bury, Peter, Bristor and Bess in 1754 to Phillis, Judy, Frank, Mary and Ned in 1805, along with two indentured servants of color, Chesa and Patty Cousins. Their names are in our transcriptions, and they are part of this family's record too.

Sources: wills of John Robards (Goochland, 1754), William Robards Sr. (Goochland, 1783) and Elizabeth Robards (Mercer Co., KY, 1805), in documents/robards-wills; widow's pension W.8562; DAR GRS A096624; Wikipedia: Lewis Robards and its sources (Little, 1913). The Lewis and Sally Robards stories come from published histories; our wills confirm they were William Sr.'s children by Elizabeth.

stories.title: Robards cousins in the history books: a congressman on both sides of the war, and a portrait painter
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Otho Robards Singleton. Otho Robards's sister Rebecca married Lewis Singleton, who ran a hemp factory near Keene in Jessamine County. In October 1814 they named their son after her little brother: Otho Robards Singleton. (William Robards Jr.'s widow named Rebecca as "wife of Lewis Singleton" in her pension application.) Young Otho studied at St. Joseph's College in Bardstown and at the Transylvania law school, then went south to practice law in Canton, Mississippi, in 1838. He served in both houses of the Mississippi legislature and was elected to Congress in 1853 and again in 1857. When Mississippi left the Union in January 1861, he walked out of the House, served as a captain in the 18th Mississippi Infantry, and then sat in the Confederate Congress for the whole war. Afterward Mississippi sent him back to Washington, and he served in the U.S. House again from 1875 to 1887, one of the few men to sit in both Congresses. He died in Washington in January 1889 and is buried in Canton.

Matthew Harris Jouett. Jack Jouett and Sallie Robards (the midnight ride is in the Jouett side quest) had a son, Matthew Harris Jouett, born in Mercer County in 1788, a half first cousin of Otho Robards. His father wanted a lawyer; Matthew wanted to paint. In the War of 1812 he served as an officer in the 28th U.S. Infantry and survived the disaster at Frenchtown, on the River Raisin, in January 1813. When a $6,000 company payroll went missing, he paid it back out of his own painting earnings. In 1816 he went to Boston to study with Gilbert Stuart, the man who painted the George Washington on the dollar bill. Back in Lexington he became the leading portrait painter of the early West, painting Henry Clay and, for the Kentucky legislature, the Marquis de Lafayette. He died in Lexington in 1827, only 39. His portraits hang today at Transylvania University, the Speed Art Museum in Louisville and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

Sources: William Robards Jr. widow's pension application (names Rebecca Singleton); Biographical Directory of the U.S. Congress (Otho R. Singleton); Matthew Harris Jouett, Wikipedia and museum records; J. H. Robards, History and Genealogy of the Robards Family.

stories.title: Lewis C. Robards: a Lexington slave trader in the family
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Not every relative in the history books is one to be proud of. Lewis C. Robards (born about 1817) was a grandson of Lewis Robards, Rachel Jackson's first husband, through his son George Lewis Robards, who was wounded with Andrew Jackson at New Orleans in 1815. That makes him a half second cousin of Otho Robards's son Younger. In the 1840s and 1850s, Lexington was one of the biggest slave markets in the upper South. Kentucky's hemp and tobacco farms had more enslaved workers than they needed, and traders bought them up and shipped them down the river to the cotton and sugar plantations around Natchez and New Orleans.

Lewis C. began as an agent for other traders with his brother Alfred, and around 1849 he opened his own jail on Short Street in Lexington, in a converted old theater. Men, women and children were held there in crowded rooms until a buyer or a downriver shipment took them. The upper floors were furnished with carpets and good furniture, where buyers came to look over young, light-skinned women sold as "fancy girls," a polite word for women sold for sexual exploitation. An Illinois lawyer, Orville Browning, toured the jail in 1854 and wrote in his diary that a young woman there was priced at $1,600.

He was also in the courts again and again. Buyers sued him for selling people he swore were "sound" who were sick or dying. In 1850 he was accused of paying a man $600 to kidnap Arian Belle, a free woman, and her four-year-old daughter Martha from Mason County and ship them south on a steamboat, until friends went to court to bring them back. Henrietta Wood, a free woman living in Cincinnati, was kidnapped across the river in 1853 and sold into slavery in Mississippi and Texas; she later named Robards in her lawsuit as one of the men behind it. She survived, came back to Ohio after the war, and in 1878 a federal jury awarded her $2,500 against another of the kidnappers, the largest known sum ever won in an American court as restitution for slavery. Her story is told in W. Caleb McDaniel's Pulitzer Prize-winning Sweet Taste of Liberty (2019).

Robards's business ran partly on borrowed money, including $6,100 from John Hunt Morgan, the future Confederate raider, who sued him and won. In 1855 the sheriff sold his jail to the big interstate firm of Bolton, Dickens & Co. By 1870 he was living with his old father near Smith Mills, in Henderson County.

Sources: J. H. Robards, History and Genealogy of the Robards Family (1910), pp. 32–33; J. Winston Coleman, Slavery Times in Kentucky (1940), pp. 157–163; Frederic Bancroft, Slave Trading in the Old South; O. H. Browning diary (1854); W. Caleb McDaniel, Sweet Taste of Liberty (2019); 1860 and 1870 censuses.

stories.title: The Pitts family: a young widow and a family still being traced
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Otho's wife, Cassandra "Cassa" Pitts (1802–1891), was born in Scott County, Kentucky, the Bluegrass county around Georgetown and Great Crossings. Before she married Otho she was already a widow: the Robards family history says her first husband was Dr. Gregg of Scott County. She outlived Otho by more than thirty years and died at 89 in Nicholasville. She named a son Younger Pitts Robards after her own family, and that son is our direct ancestor.

Her father, Younger R. Pitts, died in Scott County in November 1822. A Pitts family typescript says his widow signed the administration bond on 2 December 1822 as "Elizabeth Todd Pitts". That conflicts with the tree, which calls her Elizabeth Rogers, so her maiden name is still an open question. The typescript also traces the family to an earlier Younger Rogers Pitts, born about 1758 in Lunenburg County, Virginia, but nothing in our files proves that link yet.

A girl inside Bryan's Station. A published family history names Cassa's parents as "Younger and Elizabeth (Rogers) Pitts, of Scott Co., Ky." and says Elizabeth "was a young girl in the fort at Bryan's Station." In August 1782, a force of several hundred British-allied warriors besieged that stockade near Lexington. The fort's spring was outside the walls, and the women and girls famously walked out with buckets to fetch water, betting that the hidden attackers wouldn't fire and give away their ambush. They didn't. Days later the relief force, Daniel Boone among them, chased the attackers to the Battle of Blue Licks, where Boone's son Israel was killed. Whether Elizabeth, then a small child, carried a bucket herself is family lore. The "Todd" and "Rogers" puzzle turns out to have a simple answer: a 1946 history of the Forks of Elkhorn Church calls her Elizabeth Todd Rogers, the daughter of John and Susan Rogers of Scott County.

Labeled "Elizabeth Todd Rogers" in a MyHeritage tree. The ruffled cap and shawl fit the 1850s or early 1860s, and Elizabeth lived until June 1865, so the label is plausible, though not proven.

The Pitts estate. Younger and Elizabeth did well. By 1820 they held about 1,500 acres in Scott County. When Younger died in November 1822, Elizabeth signed the administration bond for $24,000, a sum usually set at about twice the estate's value, and his goods sold at auction in February 1823 for $12,654. Their son-in-law William C. Offutt, husband of the oldest daughter Malissa, ran the estate, and each of the seven children inherited 45 acres. Elizabeth added land from her own father's will in 1829. The last of the "Pitts land" in Kentucky, 637 acres, sold in 1860 for $50,983.

The seven heirs. Younger died without a will, so the county court had to step in. Before his death, he and a neighbor, Elijah Woolfolk, had promised Elijah Thornberry 20 acres on the head waters of Dry Run at $4 an acre. In October 1823 the court appointed commissioners to sign the deed for his heirs, and the deed lists all seven: Malissa (Mrs. W. C. Offutt), Cassa, "who has intermarried with Gregg," John Albert, Demerilla, Permilla, Younger, and Elizabeth. That one line about Cassa is the record that ties her to Younger. The younger children stayed in their mother's care. In January 1831 the court checked Elizabeth's accounts as their guardian and noted that she had charged young Younger just $100 for his board and schooling over four years. The committee called that "very moderate." That boy was the future Reverend Younger R. Pitts.

What the appraisers found. In February 1823 the appraisers walked through the Pitts farm and wrote down everything in it, and their list gives a picture of the household. There were beds hung with curtains, a looking glass, a desk and books, silver spoons, decanters and tumblers, and a set of Liverpool plates and china. Outside were thirty fat hogs, sheep, stacks of hay, hemp and hemp seed, whiskey barrels, ploughs, and a bay horse called Ballard. The list also names the people the family enslaved: Agnes, Charity, William, David, Mary Ann, Eliza Jane, Edmund, Jordan and others, appraised like property. Elizabeth bought most of the household goods back at the sale, including her own feather beds, the cows, the oxen and cart, and the books. The estate came to $12,654.25. Over the next few years the court split the estate among the children. Elizabeth, signing as "Elizabeth T. Pitts," raised the three youngest. A neighbor, William Rodes, became guardian of John Albert and Demerilla. Their accounts record William and Aggy being hired out to earn money for the children.

Cassa's brother, the preacher. Her youngest brother, Younger Rogers Pitts (1812–1871), joined the Great Crossings Baptist Church in Scott County in 1833. He held out against ordination for years, finally gave in on 17 November 1841, and became the church's pastor. In 1844 the church released him to serve as an Agent for Indian Missions. He later moderated the Elkhorn Association, Kentucky's oldest Baptist association, then moved to Missouri and pastored churches at Glasgow and Fayette. He died in 1871 while attending the Baptist General Association meeting at Clinton, Missouri, and is buried at Huntsville.

Sources: Hearne family history, p. 405 (secondary); Bradley, history of Great Crossings Church in the Elkhorn Association minutes (1876), Baptist History Homepage.

A family legend we've set aside: online trees attach Yorkshire, England, parish records for a George Pitt, who was christened in 1727, married an Elizabeth Rogers in 1747, and was buried there in 1766. A man buried in Yorkshire is very unlikely to be the father of a boy born in Virginia in 1758, so we've marked these as belonging to someone else.

Sources: Robards, History and Genealogy of the Robards Family (about 1906), p. 21; Pitts family typescript of Scott Co., KY records (documents/pitts); Yorkshire register images reviewed Nov 18. Scott Co. deed of 30 Oct 1823 from the heirs of Younger Pitts to Elijah Thornberry, and Scott Co. guardian settlements recorded 17 Jan 1831, both found on FamilySearch (free).

stories.title: Uncle Daniel Everhart and "the prettiest home in the county"
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
George Robards's mother, Nancy White Everhart (1848–1913), was the daughter of Daniel Everhart and Eliza Bodine of Marion County, Kentucky. An old reminiscence in the Lebanon Enterprise, "The Everharts of Marion County in the Early Days," remembered "Uncle Daniel" as a wealthy man and slaveholder with "the prettiest home in the county": a big white frame house on the Campbellsville turnpike, three miles from Lebanon. The family were Presbyterians. Local lore even says Aaron Burr once stopped there; that's a legend, not a record. Daniel died in 1861, and the Louisville Daily Journal advertised the estate sale "at the late residence of Daniel Everhart, dec'd" for 1 October 1861. Oil portraits of Daniel and Eliza survive.

Eliza's Bodine family. Eliza was the daughter of Charles Bodine (1780–1819), and she married Daniel Everhart in Nelson County on 14 October 1840, when she was 29; the marriage register names her father, Charles. Charles had died at 38 in January 1819, leaving his widow Elizabeth to run the farm and act as administratrix. His inventory reads like a picture of a Kentucky farm of the time: horses (one of them blind), cattle, twenty sheep, a loom, shoemaker's tools, and two stills with their worms and caps, so the Bodines made their own whiskey. It also lists five enslaved people: Betty, Peggy and her child Harriet, Mary, Presley and Frank.

Elizabeth was a Stone, and her father's will tells a story. Elizabeth's father was Davis Stone, who came to Nelson County from Fairfax County, Virginia, where in January 1792 he and Rebeckah Stone had been executors of Eli Stone's will. Davis's own will, recorded in Nelson County in late 1827, settles who Elizabeth was. It leaves $400 to "my daughter Elizabeth Stone now Elizabeth Bodine" and $50 each to her children William, Nancy, Sally, Eliza and Elizabeth Bodine. His son Isaac D. Stone got land on the East Fork of Simpson's Creek "with the new still house", so Eliza had whiskey makers on both sides of her family. The most striking lines are about two other sons. Davis left James and John Stone $400 each "should they ever make their personal appearance" and ordered that the money "is never to be paid to any representative whatever." Two of his boys had gone off, probably west, and the family no longer knew whether they were alive. Davis also remembered the children of three children who had died before him (Nancy White, William D. Stone and Edward D. Stone), and he asked that the farm stay "a nursery and place of retreat and support for my wife and children."

Elizabeth and Charles had married in Nelson County on 3 June 1805, and the county marriage record also names her father, Davis Stone.

Sources: will of Davis Stone, Nelson Co., KY will book pp. 238–239 (1827); Fairfax Co., VA will book pp. 56–57 (1792). Saved in documents/stone/.

Charles's father Isaac Bodine left a will that turned into a small family drama. Isaac signed it on 5 October 1816 with only one witness, which made it legally invalid. When he died in 1818, his children could have fought over the estate. Instead, every one of them, Charles, Cornelius, Isaac, Asher, Jacob, and the sons-in-law Elsworth Owsley and Richard Skinner with their wives, signed agreements saying they were "perfectly satisfied with our father's disposal of his property" and would abide by it "in all things," because "he believed & intended it to be a valid will." Isaac left his wife Elizabeth (Pullen) the plantation for life. One of the witnesses to the children's agreement was an Asher Pullen, from her side of the family. Charles honored his sister too: he named a daughter Mary Skinner Bodine.

Sources: Nelson Co. KY will book, Isaac Bodine will and heirs' agreements (recorded 16 Nov 1818); inventory of Charles Bodine (Feb.–Sept. 1819); DAR typescript, Record of Marriages in Nelson County 1780–1851, p. 31; Bodine family Bible (published 1963).

Nancy (Everhart) Robards (1848–1913), Uncle Daniel's daughter and George Robards's mother, in her later years, about 1900–1910.

Daniel Everhart's oil portrait, from the family tree photos.

Daniel's father, Martin Everhart, came from Maryland. A 1799 Baltimore County deed shows Martin and his wife Sarah McAllister, by then living in Washington County, Kentucky, selling land called "Darbyshire" that Sarah's relative James McAllister had given her in 1786.

stories.title: Johannes Theodorus Polhemus: from the Palatinate and Dutch Brazil to Flatbush
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
One of the deepest and best-documented roots in the tree runs from Nancy Everhart's mother, Eliza Bodine, back through five generations of Bodines and Sebrings to a Dutch Reformed minister who preached in three languages on two continents.

A refugee minister. Johannes Theodorus Polhemus was born about 1598 at "Boikirchen" in the German Palatinate and enrolled at Heidelberg University in January 1620, just as the Thirty Years' War broke over the Palatinate. He later told the church authorities in Amsterdam that he had twice been driven out of the Palatinate by persecution. By 1624 he was preaching in Drenthe, in the northern Netherlands, learning Dutch as he went, and from 1627 he was minister at Meppel and head of its Latin school.

Sugar, war and slavery in Dutch Brazil. In December 1635 he signed on with the Dutch West India Company and sailed for Brazil on the ship Haerlem. The Dutch had seized the sugar coast of Pernambuco from Portugal, and he spent eighteen years there as a minister at Cabo de Santo Agostinho, Goiana, Fort Ceulen on the Rio Grande and Paraíba, and longest on the island of Itamaracá, preaching in Dutch, French and Portuguese. There he married Catharina van Werven, and there their children were born, among them Adrianna, about 1644. Brazil's sugar ran on enslaved labor, and the minister was part of that world: he owned a sugar plantation on Itamaracá until he sold it in 1645, and the colony's records show him buying and selling enslaved people.

1654: two escapes. In January 1654 the Portuguese took back Recife, and the Dutch had to leave. Catharina and the children went home to the Netherlands. Johannes sailed north to New Amsterdam, arriving by early September 1654. A fellow minister wrote that "some Jews" came with him: that was the same month that 23 Jewish refugees from Recife landed at New Amsterdam and founded the first Jewish community in North America.

The first minister of Flatbush. That October he began preaching at Midwout (Flatbush) in what is now Brooklyn, at first without pay, and Peter Stuyvesant's council soon had a church built there. From 1656 he also served Breuckelen (Brooklyn) and Amersfoort (Flatlands). His family joined him in 1656 on the Gulden Otter, and his letters to Amsterdam complain of unpaid salary and a house so unfinished that his family slept in the cold. He kept the pulpit for 22 years. When he died on 8 June 1676, he was buried in front of the pulpit, and the church book called him its "dear, loyal old shepherd and teacher." Catharina lived on in Flatbush until about 1702.

stories.title: Jacob Bodine and Elizabeth Sebring: Huguenots on the way to Kentucky
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
The Bodines. Elizabeth Sebring married Jacob Bodine of Staten Island. Staten Island's Bodines were French Huguenots, Protestants who fled France as Louis XIV turned on them in the 1680s. Jacob and Elizabeth settled at Six Mile Run in Somerset County, New Jersey, a Dutch farming settlement on the Raritan, where their son Cornelius was born in 1723. Cornelius took the family south to Loudoun County, Virginia, where he died in 1781, the year of Yorktown. His son Isaac Addison Bodine, born in Loudoun in 1752, married there in 1777 and then joined the great migration over the mountains to Nelson County, Kentucky, where he died in 1818. Isaac's son Charles, with his two whiskey stills, and Charles's daughter Eliza carry the story on in Kentucky.

Sources: New York Genealogical and Biographical Society, New Netherland Settlers: Johannes Theodorus Polhemius and Catharina van Werven (citing Seversmith 1955, Peck in the NYG&B Record 1959–61, and Amsterdam classis and Dutch council records); Henry Hoff, "Genealogies of Long Island Families," NYG&B Record (1987); Polhemus letter to the Classis of Amsterdam, 4 Jun 1658, in Ecclesiastical Records of the State of New York; Bodine wills and guardianship records, Nelson Co., KY.

stories.title: John Hurst (1713–1789) of Accotink Run
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Sally Dulin, the Fairfax County girl who married Davis Stone in 1781, came from two old northern Virginia families. Her father's and grandfather's wills, written ten years apart, show the families just before their children began moving west to Kentucky.

John Hurst (1713–1789), Sally's grandfather, was born on Accotink Run in what was then Stafford County and farmed in Fairfax County for most of his life. His first wife, Elizabeth Summers, died in 1781. He wrote his will on 10 March 1787, with a second wife, Sybil, at his side. It leaves Sybil the home plantation, its furniture, two horses, a woman's saddle, an oval table, a looking glass and "one large Bible" for her life. After her death it was all to be divided equally among the children.

The will reads like a map of his land deals. Son James got the land John had bought from William and James Saunders, on one condition: James could not turn William Follin off the place he lived on, or charge him rent, for seven years. Follin was probably a son-in-law, since John's daughter Bathsheba was a Follin. Son William got the land bought from George Thrift, and daughter Susanna got the land bought from John Gunnell. A rented plantation on the Sugar Lands was to pay rent to all the children. John also held a warrant for 1,000 acres of land not yet surveyed; the transcript is unclear about where it was. That was to be shared by James, William, Susanna and Jane Williams. The rest of the estate was to be sold, with Sybil to get one child's share "and no more." The other children named are Elizabeth Thrift and Sarah Dulin, Sally's mother, plus a granddaughter, Elizabeth Marshal.

The will also divided more than a dozen enslaved men, women and children among Sybil, the children and the granddaughter. Several mothers were passed on with their youngest children "and their increase", the legal phrase that claimed any children born to them later. Sally's mother received an enslaved girl. The family's research notes keep their names, since for their own descendants a will like this is often the only record of them.

The executors were Sybil, son James, and Jeremiah Williams, who was married to John's daughter Jane. The witnesses were Love Lewis, Aaron Ally and Mary Sewell. The Dulin family Bible says John died on 5 November at age 73; the year is torn away. (The family tree has 26 April 1789.) James brought the will into the Fairfax court on 21 December 1789. That day he posted a £3,500 bond as executor, with George Thrift, Henry Gunnell and William Hunter Jr. as his sureties. The bond is copied on the facing page of the will book.

stories.title: Edward Dulin (about 1719–1782) and Sarah Hurst
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html:
Edward Dulin (about 1719–1782), Sally's father, was born probably in King George County, Virginia; the family tree says Essex County, 1720. He married John Hurst's daughter Sarah Hurst in the 1750s. In July 1765, when Truro Parish was split in two, Edward was elected a vestryman of the new Fairfax Parish. George Washington was elected to the Truro Parish vestry the same week. A descendant recorded that the family remembered him as "Judge Dulin," though no one knows whether he was a lawyer or a justice. Edward wrote his will on 12 February 1778, in the middle of the Revolution, and it was proved on 18 November 1782. The Dulin family Bible gives his death as 20 September 1782, at age 63. The will names his wife Sarah; sons William, Edward and John; and daughters Elizabeth (wife of John Summers), Anne and Sally. Sarah, son William and son-in-law John Summers were the executors. Jeremiah Williams witnessed this will too, so the same brother-in-law stood by both families.

The Dulin family Bible, owned in the 1960s by a descendant in South Carolina, records exact dates for many of Edward and Sarah's descendants. Unusually for a family Bible, it also records the births and deaths of many of the people the family enslaved. Edward's will is also indexed in Enslaved.org's Fairfax County probate records. Sarah outlived Edward by eighteen years and died in Fairfax on 31 May 1800, leaving a spoken (nuncupative) will.

Sally, born 13 March 1765, was the fourth of six children, after William (1757), Elizabeth (1760) and Anne (1762), and before Edward Jr. (1769) and John (1771). She married Davis Stone in October 1781, the year before her father died. The couple later took her Fairfax roots over the mountains to Nelson County, Kentucky, where Sally died in 1813. She is buried in the Stone Cemetery near Bloomfield.

Sources: will of John Hurst and executor's bond, Fairfax Co., VA, Will Book E, Part 1 (1783–1791), pp. 348–349, recorded 21 Dec 1789 (FamilySearch Full-Text Search, image 221). Will of Edward Dulin, Fairfax Co. Will Book D-1 (1776–1782), pp. 298–301. Roberta Dulin Stewart, The Dulin Family in America (1961), ch. VI, which quotes the Dulin family Bible and Philip Slaughter, History of Truro Parish (1907), p. 45. FamilySearch also lists a 1790 Fairfax deed-book lawsuit of John Hurst's heirs and an 1849 Fairfax suit over the Follin children. To confirm: Sarah Dulin's 1800 will, the 1790 heirs' suit, and where John Hurst's 1,000-acre warrant lay.

stories.title: Anna Maria Haskamp (born 1815) of Harpendorf
stories.group: Donna's father's side: a Union soldier, Kentucky gentry, and a cousin who married Charles Eames
stories.html: Catherine's mother, Anna Maria Haskamp. Catherine's mother came from farther north. Anna Maria Haskamp was born on 9 May 1815 at Harpendorf, in the parish of Damme, in the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg, the daughter of Johann Bernard Haskamp (1779–1845) and Anna Margaretha Bocklage (1777–1853). Damme lies under the wooded Dammer Hills in the Catholic "Oldenburg Münsterland," poor, sandy farm country. For generations its young men walked to Holland every summer to cut hay and dig peat as hired hands, and in the 1830s and 1840s whole families went to America instead, many of them to Missouri. Her parents stayed behind and died at Damme. Anna Maria married Christian Schwiering in St. Louis on 18 March 1842. When he died on 1 September 1872, she signed his death notice as "the grieving wife," with their son Johann, daughter Lizzie, and sons-in-law Georg Wetsel and W. H. Woermann. She died on 3 May 1883, aged 68, and her son-in-law Woermann handled her estate. Both are buried at St. Peter's Cemetery in Normandy. Also spelled: Haskamp, Hascamp, Haschkamp, Hasekamp; Bocklage, Bockelage.

stories.title: Frederick C. Woermann and the cousin who married Charles Eames

stories.html:
The famous cousin: Minnie's younger brother Frederick Christian Woermann (born 1877) did well enough to build a house at 7 Arundel Place in St. Louis, designed by the architect William B. Ittner. The Library of Congress has documented it as the Fred and Lucia Woermann House. In 1929 Fred's daughter Catherine Woermann married a young architecture student she'd met at Washington University: Charles Eames, who went on to design the Eames chair. They had a daughter, Lucia, and divorced in 1941. So the Eames chair sits one branch over in Donna's family: Catherine was a first cousin of Donna's grandmother Eleanor.

stories.title: Uncle Robert: the brother who didn't come home
stories.group: Donna's mother's side: a B-24 gunner, a double house on Pennsylvania Avenue, and wine-country Germans
stories.html:
The most moving story in this branch belongs to Jean's big brother, Staff Sergeant Robert Julius Mueller Jr., born 12 July 1922 in St. Louis. He was Donna's uncle.

When his parents divorced, Robert went to live with his father and was raised mostly by his grandmother, Laura, while Jean stayed with their mother, Elsa. He entered the Army on 17 March 1943, trained as an aerial gunner, and by the summer of 1944 was a staff sergeant in the 566th Bomb Squadron, 389th Bomb Group, flying B-24 Liberators out of Hethel airfield near Norwich, England.

The last mission, 7 July 1944. That morning the Eighth Air Force sent its heavy bombers deep into central Germany, against the aircraft factories and oil plants around Halle and Bernburg. Robert flew as a gunner aboard the Liberator nicknamed "Sack Warmer," serial 41-28824. The B-24 groups met some of the fiercest fighter attacks of that summer. Twin-engine Ju 88s and Me 410s came in from the side firing rockets and cannon, and a pack of about thirty Fw 190s hit the formations from behind, firing time-fused shells from about 1,200 yards. A neighboring group, the 492nd, reportedly lost twelve Liberators that day, and the 392nd lost six. Sack Warmer was hit by rockets, caught fire and exploded, and came down at about 9:30 a.m. near the village of Brumby, close to Calbe on the Saale. Eight of the ten men aboard were killed. Only the navigator and the tail gunner got out, and they spent the rest of the war as prisoners. Robert was 21, five days short of his 22nd birthday.

How the family found out. The War Department reported him killed in action on 17 August 1944. In September 1944 the Germans passed a casualty list through the American legation in Bern, Switzerland, naming Robert and crewmates including Paul R. Brown, Ernest R. Brown, Floyd S. Collins, Elmer R. Olson, Everett O. Scott and Alton Reed. The burgomaster of Brumby reported that the airmen had been buried in the village cemetery on 8 July, the day after the crash. Robert's personal effects reached his father in 1945: his watch, rings and bracelets, pens, a hunting knife, two prayer books, two photo albums, and his letters and photographs. After the war the Army moved him to the new American cemetery at Margraten, Holland, ten miles west of Aachen, to Plot X, Row 11, Grave 270, under a wooden cross.

S/Sgt Robert J. Mueller Jr., as pictured in a St. Louis newspaper.

The family's grief is all over his file. In 1946 his father wrote asking whether "my dear son's" grave had been found. In 1950, when the Army offered to bring him home, his father chose to have him returned. His mother Elsa, who had remarried, wrote to the Army that September so the record would show the truth: she had let Robert go to his father only because she had to go out to work and wanted him raised by his grandmother instead of strangers. "I loved Robert just as much as Jean," she wrote. On 29 September 1950 Robert was reburied at Jefferson Barracks National Cemetery in St. Louis, where his father would later join him.

Kristin got his 99-page file free from the National Archives at St. Louis, and it also proves that Robert and Jean were full brother and sister.

Sources: Individual Deceased Personnel File, S/Sgt Robert J. Mueller Jr., ASN 37608089 (National Archives at St. Louis); Missing Air Crew Report 7363; casualty list and photo from a St. Louis newspaper; headstone at Jefferson Barracks; "Bringing Him Home" file in documents/mueller. The 389th Bomb Group has a veterans' site with crew records.

stories.title: Jean Mueller Koetter (1928–?): close to both her fathers
stories.group: Donna's mother's side: a B-24 gunner, a double house on Pennsylvania Avenue, and wine-country Germans
stories.html:
Jean Mueller was born in St. Louis in 1928, the daughter of Robert Julius Mueller Sr. and Elsa Schepflin. When her parents divorced, Jean stayed with her mother, and her big brother Robert went to their father and grandmother. Robert was killed over Germany in July 1944, when Jean was about 16. In 1950 her mother wrote to the Army, "I loved Robert just as much as Jean." Elsa later married Victor Dittrich, and some records call Jean by his surname. Jean stayed very close to both of her fathers, Robert Mueller and Victor Dittrich, all her life.

Jean married Vernon Koetter. In 1961, living in California, she gave the details for her mother's death certificate. She and Vern retired to their farm near Montgomery City, Missouri, and she is buried beside him at Bethel Methodist Cemetery.

Sources: Robert J. Mueller Jr.'s personnel file; Elsa Dittrich's 1961 death certificate; family memories.

stories.title: The Muellers and Schulers: a quarryman's son born in Alabama
stories.group: Donna's mother's side: a B-24 gunner, a double house on Pennsylvania Avenue, and wine-country Germans
stories.html:
Jean's father, Robert Julius Mueller Sr. (1892–1959), was the son of Anton Mueller and Laura Schuler. Anton is a puzzle worth noticing: he was born on 6 March 1858 in Alabama, to German parents, before the family settled in St. Louis. His father Andrew Mueller worked as a quarryman, and his mother Margaret lived to 85.

The Muellers and Schulers ended up living side by side in a double house at 4733–4735 Pennsylvania Avenue. Laura's mother, Caroline Arnold Schuler, died there in 1915. Anton's mother Margaret died next door in 1917, with Anton as the informant. Anton died there too, in 1930. Robert Sr. was still at 4733 when he wrote to the Army about his son.

Caroline Arnold came from Bedesbach, a village in the Palatinate (Pfalz), the daughter of Michael Arnold and Catharina Pfeiffer. Her husband Albert Schuler was from Saxony; they married in St. Louis on 2 April 1866, the year after the Civil War ended.

Sources: death certificates of Anton Mueller (1930), Margareth Mueller (1917), Caroline Schuler (1915), Laura Mueller (1954) and Robert Mueller (1959), all free on Missouri Digital Heritage; 1866 St. Louis marriage; 1880 census.

stories.title: The Arnolds of the Glan valley: a mason married under Napoleon, and a ship to New Orleans
stories.group: Donna's mother's side: a B-24 gunner, a double house on Pennsylvania Avenue, and wine-country Germans
stories.html:
Also spelled: Arnold, Arnhold; Jean, Johannes, John; Moehn, Möhn, Mehn; Pfeiffer, Pfeifer; Catharina, Katharina, Catherine; Karolina, Caroline.

Caroline Arnold Schuler's people came from the Kusel district in the far west of the Palatinate (Pfalz), a string of small farm villages along the little Glan river, between Kaiserslautern and the French border. It is hilly, stony country. The farms were too small to feed big families, so the sons became masons and quarrymen, and later in the century, travelling musicians who took brass bands all over the world. The district still calls itself the "Musikantenland."

A wedding in the French Republic. Caroline's grandfather Jean Arnold was born at Rammelsbach, just outside Kusel, on 24 June 1778, the son of Johannes Arnold and Marie Elisabethe Weisenstein. By the time he married, his homeland was not German at all. French revolutionary armies had taken the left bank of the Rhine in the 1790s, and Kusel was now part of the French Département de la Sarre. So his marriage record is written in French and dated by the Revolutionary calendar: 22 Fructidor, Year XIII, which is 9 September 1805. The groom is "Jean Arnold, maçon," a mason, aged 27. The bride is Marie Elisabethe Moehn, 21, born on 1 May 1784 at nearby Rathsweiler, the daughter of Jacques Moehn and the late Catherine Cloos. Her father stood by to give his consent. Less than three months later, Napoleon won his great victory at Austerlitz. Their son Michael, born on 6 April 1810, was born a French subject. When he was six, the Congress of Vienna handed the district to the Kingdom of Bavaria, and the Palatinate stayed Bavarian for more than a century.

Michael and Catharina. Catharina Pfeiffer was born on 25 September 1819 at Ulmet, a few miles down the Glan, the daughter of Nickel (Nikolaus) Pfeiffer and Maria Elisabetha Hennemann, and baptized there on 3 October. She and Michael were married by the civil registrar on 19 March 1845. They lived at Bedesbach, where their daughter Karolina was born that October.

Why they left. The 1840s were hungry years in the Palatinate. Potato blight and failed harvests in 1846 and 1847 drove up the price of bread, and in 1849 the Palatinate rose in revolt against the Bavarian king, a rising that Prussian troops crushed within weeks. In the years that followed, tens of thousands of Palatines left for America. A passenger list shows Michael Arnhold, about 43, of Bavaria, sailing from Le Havre and landing at New Orleans on 9 March 1853. That was the usual road for the Palatines: overland to the French coast, across the Atlantic, and then a week or more by steamboat up the Mississippi to St. Louis. We don't yet know whether Catharina and seven-year-old Caroline sailed with him or followed later. That same year a young Peter Arnold left Rammelsbach to join relatives in New York, probably another of the family.

By 1860 the Arnholds were living in the 1st Ward of St. Louis. Caroline married Albert Schuler in 1866, and her story goes on in the section above. Michael died in 1884. Catharina was still in the city in the late 1880s, living on Sidney Street on the south side.

Still to find: the full 1853 passenger list page, which should name the ship and show whether the family travelled together; the image of the 1845 civil marriage; and Michael's and Catharina's death records in St. Louis.

Sources: Kusel marriage act, 22 Fructidor an XIII (9 Sep 1805); Ulmet baptism index, 1819; Bedesbach marriage and birth indexes, 1845 (FamilySearch, free); New Orleans passenger list index, 9 Mar 1853 (Ancestry); 1860 census, St. Louis; Caroline Schuler's 1915 death certificate. Copies in documents/arnold-pfeiffer.

stories.title: The Schoepflins of Bahlingen, in Baden's wine country
stories.group: Donna's mother's side: a B-24 gunner, a double house on Pennsylvania Avenue, and wine-country Germans
stories.html:
Jean's mother, Elsa Schepflin (1900–1961), was the daughter of Charles F. Schepflin and Mathilda Ultzen. Charles was born Karl Friedrich Schöpflin on 18 September 1860 in Bahlingen am Kaiserstuhl, a wine village in the Upper Rhine valley of Baden, near the French border. The Kaiserstuhl is an old volcanic hill famous for its vineyards and some of the warmest weather in Germany. His parents, Georg Michael Schöpflin and Anna Maria Schmidt, had married in the Bahlingen Protestant church on 24 January 1856.

The family emigrated, and by 1880 Anna Maria was a widow living in Meramec Township, Jefferson County, Missouri, with her son Charles. Her own family, the Schmidts, can be traced in the parish books of nearby Nimburg and Teningen back to the early 1700s.

The grandparents in Bahlingen and Teningen. Georg Michael Schöpflin was born on 3 January 1829 in Bahlingen, the son of Michael Schöpflin (1802–1874) and Catharina Stäublin (1807–1876), who married in the Bahlingen church on 8 February 1829, a month after he was born. That was not unusual in Baden, where a couple often had to prove they could support a family before the authorities would let them marry. Michael's own father, also Michael Schöpflin, had died in 1809, when his son was seven; his mother was Salome Morizin. Catharina's father, Johann Georg Stäublin (1772–1844), came from Gundelfingen, just north of Freiburg, and her mother was Catharina Kaufmann. On the other side, Anna Maria Schmidt was born on 13 August 1829 in Teningen, the daughter of Gottfried Schmidt (1793–1854), born in Nimburg, and Maria Catharina Limberger (1793–1842) of Teningen, who married in 1818. Anna Maria lost her mother at twelve and her father at 24, so both were gone by her wedding. Gottfried's parents, Jakob Friedrich Schmidt (1763–1815) and Catharina Schumacher (1770–1846), had married at Nimburg in 1791, and Maria Catharina's were Johann Wilhelm Limberger and Anna Barbara Fuchs. All these villages lie within a dozen miles of each other, on the plain between the Kaiserstuhl and the Black Forest. They were Protestant villages in a mostly Catholic corner of Germany, because they had belonged to the margraves of Baden-Durlach, who turned Lutheran in 1556. Also spelled: Schöpflin, Schoepflin, Schepflin; Stäublin, Staeublin; Fuchs, Fuechs; Morizin, Moritz.

Elsa's St. Louis. When Elsa was born on 28 July 1900, her father Charles was working as a carpenter, and the family lived in a red-brick house at 1706 Allen Avenue on the south side of St. Louis. The house is still standing. She grew up at 3710 South Jefferson Avenue, which also still stands; another house she lived in as a girl is now the site of a school. Her father died in 1908, before she turned ten, and left Mathilda a widow with five children under fourteen: Ida, Edward, Hulda, Elsa and Julius. The city directories show the family moving every few years, often into rented rooms, and those must have been hard years. Mathilda later remarried and died in 1937 as Mathilda Kleb. Elsa grew up to be remembered in the family as a classy lady who could play the piano by ear, and her piano is still in the family today. She died in St. Louis on 28 June 1961 and is buried at New St. Marcus Cemetery in Affton.

Sources: Bahlingen marriage index (1856) and baptism index (1860), free on FamilySearch; 1880 census, Jefferson Co., MO; death certificates of Mathilda Kleb (1937) and Elsa Dittrich (1961).

stories.title: The Ultzens and Kropps: from Herford to the Meramec
stories.group: Donna's mother's side: a B-24 gunner, a double house on Pennsylvania Avenue, and wine-country Germans
stories.html:
Mathilda Ultzen was born in 1869 in Jefferson County, Missouri, the daughter of Diederich Ultzen, from the Kingdom of Hanover, and Emma Kropp, born in 1842 in Herford, Westphalia. Emma's father, Friedrich August Kropp, appears on Herford's list of emigrants, leaving for St. Louis in 1852. He died within a few years, and the 1860 census finds Emma living with her widowed mother, Henriette Haase Kropp, in Meramec Township.

Henriette's people: the linen country around Bielefeld. Henriette Wilhelmine Haase was born on 29 August 1818 at Milse, a farm village just outside Bielefeld, the daughter of Conrad Ditrich Haase (born 1788 in Heepen) and Friederike Wilhelmine Warrentrup (born 1795 in Heepen). Friederike's parents, Johann Friedrich Warrentrup and Anna Ilsabe Oldemeyers, married in the Lutheran church at Heepen in 1791, aged 21 and 22. This was the old county of Ravensberg, famous across Europe for its linen. Almost every farmhouse grew flax, and the family spun and wove through the winter for the Bielefeld merchants. When cheap machine-spun yarn arrived in the 1830s and 1840s, the cottage spinners lost their living, and hunger and emigration followed. Henriette married Friedrich August Kropp of Herford, son of Johann Jodocus Kropp and Maria Carolina Froböse, in December 1837. Her father died at the end of 1849, and a few years later she and August took the children to Missouri. August died in February 1860 at Belew's Creek in Jefferson County. Henriette outlived him by almost forty years and died in St. Louis on 8 January 1899, aged 80. Also spelled: Haase, Hase; Ditrich, Dietrich; Warrentrup, Warentrup; Oldemeyers, Oldemeier; Froböse, Froboese.

Diederich died in 1884 and is buried at Saint Matthew Cemetery. Emma lived on as a widow in St. Louis. After her death in 1893, a newspaper notice of a trustee's sale for her lot on Arsenal Street was signed by William F. Kropp, probably her brother. She had signed her own papers "Emma K. Ultzen", keeping her maiden initial.

Sources: Herford emigration list, p. 527; 1837 Kropp–Haase marriage index (Schildesche); 1860 census, Meramec Twp.; St. Louis Post-Dispatch, 4 May 1894, p. 8; Find a Grave memorials 32689707 and 155700516; Mathilda Kleb's 1937 death certificate.

stories.title: Sgt. Lawrence Everhart: hero of Cowpens, and maybe kin
stories.group: Stories still being proven
stories.html: Lawrence Everhart of Frederick County, Maryland, was a cavalry sergeant under Col. William Washington. At Cowpens in January 1781 he is credited with saving Washington's life when British dragoons cut him off. Later he became a Methodist preacher, freed people he had enslaved in 1795 and 1799, and sat in a place of honor when Lafayette visited Frederick in 1824. His parents, Christian and Sybilla Eberhard, came from the Palatinate in 1764 and are buried at St. James Reformed Church in Lovettsville, Virginia (Lovettsville Historical Society). Our tree gives Martin Everhart parents with the same names, but the society's list of Lawrence's brothers doesn't include a Martin. A Martin Everhart also appears as a partner in an early Frederick glassworks. To confirm: a Loudoun or Frederick will or estate of Christian Eberhard that names a son Martin.

stories.title: The ironworks that supplied the Revolution
stories.group: Stories still being proven
stories.html:
The Washington Iron Works. On Furnace Creek, just outside today's Rocky Mount in Franklin County, Virginia, iron was being made by 1773 at a small "bloomery" run by Col. John Donelson, whose daughter Rachel later married Andrew Jackson. That year his crew was four white men and six enslaved workers. In 1779, in the middle of the Revolution, Donelson sold it to two Bedford County men, Col. James Callaway and his father-in-law Jeremiah Early. They renamed it the Washington Iron Works in honor of the commander-in-chief.

Callaway was a hard man to miss. He had served on Bedford's Committee of Safety in 1775, had run Virginia's public lead mines in the southwest of the state (lead was what musket balls were made of), and from 1778 commanded the Bedford County militia. In 1780 he and other militia officers broke up a suspected Loyalist plot at the lead mines, rough justice that is often given as the origin of the phrase "lynch law." He and Early soon built a stone blast furnace, and wartime demand made the works grow fast. By July 1779 its iron was being advertised as far away as South Carolina, and it supplied the Patriot side. When Thomas Jefferson wrote his Notes on the State of Virginia in 1781–82, he counted it as making about a quarter of Virginia's bar iron and about 14 percent of its pig iron.

Jeremiah Early died in 1779, the same year as the purchase. His share went to his sons, and by 1781 his son John had sold it to Callaway. The works kept going for another seventy years under Callaway's heirs and then the Saunders brothers, who bought it about 1820. By 1836 it employed about 100 men and made 160 tons of iron a year, hauled by wagon down the old Carolina Road. A flood on Furnace Creek cracked the furnace while it was hot in 1851 (some accounts say 1850). The 30-foot granite stack still stands. It is one of the best-preserved iron furnaces in Virginia, but it sits on private land off Old Furnace Road; state marker A-97 on South Main Street tells its story.

How it touches our family. The Earlys and the Rogers brothers were neighbors back in Culpeper County: in 1764 Jeremiah Early bought 100 acres on Beautiful Run "adjoyning to the Lands of William and Joseph Rogers." Ann Early married Joseph Hale Rogers, our John Rogers's brother, so the ironworks family were Elizabeth Rogers's aunt's people. Older family trees made Ann Early our direct ancestor, which is how this story came into the family; John Rogers's will (below) showed that Elizabeth was John's daughter, not Joseph Hale's. One puzzle is left: an SAR lineage makes Ann the daughter of Jeremiah Early Sr. (about 1705–1787), while Wikipedia gives the ironworks partner as a Jeremiah Early who lived 1730–1779. If those are two men, the ironmaster was Ann's brother rather than her father.

Sources: Wikipedia, Washington Iron Furnace; Library of Virginia, Dictionary of Virginia Biography: James Callaway; Virginia DHR register entry 157-0029; Marker A-97 on HMdb; Culpeper Deed Book D (1764); SAR application 139391.

Grandfather Rogers's will. Elizabeth's father was John Rogers of Scott County, who in 1800 sat as one of the county's justices. In his will, dated 16 December 1828, he lent his wife Susannah the farm for the rest of her life, along with the clock, the cupboard, half the earthenware, the bell-metal kettle, the tea kettle and her pick of the horses. He left his rifle to William Offutt, "who married Grand Daughter Millica Pitts," and his silver patent-lever watch to young Clifton Rogers, the son of his nephew James Rogers. To James himself he left his smooth-bore gun and Jerry, a man he held in slavery. Nearly everything else, including the neighboring tract of land and the rest of his property, went to "my Daughter Betsey Pitts," whom he named his executrix. The will was proved on 15 June 1829, and the next month Elizabeth posted her bond as executrix, with her son John A. Pitts and Cassa's new husband, Otho Robards, as her securities.

Following Jerry to find John's family. Older family trees had made Elizabeth the daughter of Joseph Hale Rogers, the famous defender of Bryan's Station. John's will showed that was wrong, but it left a clue: "my Nephew James Rogers," whom John named an executor. In 1837 a James Rogers of Fayette County wrote his own will. He left "my son Clifton R. Rogers" four enslaved people, and one of them was Jerry, the same man John had left to James eight years before. James's wife was Susan T. Rogers, and one of his daughters was married to Waller Rodes. Then, in a Fayette deed book, we found a power of attorney dated 7 November 1835 in which "Jeremiah Rogers, John Rogers, James Rogers, and Henry Rogers" appointed Henry Rogers and Waller Rodes to look after "the Estate of our decd. Father Joseph Rogers." So nephew James was Joseph Hale Rogers's son, and our John Rogers was Joseph Hale's brother. The old trees had the right family after all, just one branch off.

The Rogers brothers of Culpeper. John and Joseph Hale were sons of Joseph Rogers of Bromfield Parish, Culpeper County, Virginia, and his wife Lucy (by tradition a daughter of Thomas Burgess of Orange County). Joseph signed his will on 2 August 1761 and died the next winter. It was proved on 18 March 1762. He left land to his four sons, William, Joseph, John and Barnett, and named his daughters Frances, Ann, Sarah, Lucy and Betty. His inventory calls him "Joseph Rogers, Gent." A family history says that "the four sons went to Kentucky," and each of them left a mark there:

  • Barnett (Bernard) came out with Joseph Hale "prospecting for a home" and fought in the siege of Bryan's Station in August 1782. Three days later he was killed at the Battle of Blue Licks. His body was carried back to Bryan's Station and buried in the old Rogers graveyard.
  • Joseph Hale Rogers (1742–1834) stayed at Bryan's Station. By the end of his life he had 700 to 800 acres on both sides of Elkhorn Creek, with a grist mill, a saw mill and a whiskey still house. His tombstone says he died on 13 July 1834, "aged 92 yrs. and 4 months."
  • William Rogers (1744–1828) brought his family from Culpeper in 1785 and settled in Scott County near Georgetown. He died there in August 1828.
  • John, our ancestor, also settled in Scott County. William's death in August 1828 may be what moved John to write his own will that December.

A fight over Uncle Joseph's will. Joseph Hale Rogers married three times. In his will of 1828 he left almost everything to his third wife, Susan, and their young son, Bernard F. Rogers. One older son, Coleman, was told he had already had "upwards of Ten Thousand Dollars" and should not get "another cent." He also asked his executors to "set my old man Adam free at my death, and his wife Frank," and to care for his old servants as long as they lived. When the will was proved in September 1834, the older children went to court in chancery. On 28 May 1835 Susan agreed to give up the will. She kept the land north of the old Limestone road for her lifetime, the carriage and two horses, and the household furniture. Her stepsons Jeremiah, John, James, Henry and Richard took the rest. The settlement papers of 28 November 1835 list by name and age the enslaved people divided between them, from Grace, "about sixty," to two-year-old Joe.

stories.title: Bryan's Station and Blue Licks, 1782: the Rogers brothers in the last fight of the Revolution
stories.group: Stories still being proven
stories.html:
Cornwallis had surrendered at Yorktown in October 1781, but on the Kentucky frontier the war was not over. The British at Detroit kept arming and supplying Shawnee, Wyandot and Delaware war parties, and in the summer of 1782 they sent the biggest force Kentucky had yet seen. Two of our Rogers brothers, Joseph Hale and Barnett, were in the middle of it. A third brother, William, settled near Georgetown in 1785. One early list of the defenders, Joseph Ficklin's, also names a William Rogers, and a William Rogers Sr. and a Corporal William Rogers served in Capt. Robert Sanders's Fayette militia company in 1786. Our own John Rogers is not on any list of the defenders we have found, so we can't say where he was that August.

The fort on Elkhorn. Bryan's Station was a stockade of cabins on the south bank of the North Fork of Elkhorn Creek, about five miles northeast of the new settlement of Lexington. A family history quoting George Ranck's History of Bryan's Station says a 1774 survey already showed the land belonging to Joseph Rogers of Virginia. Joseph Hale Rogers and his brother Barnett had come out from Culpeper "the year before the siege," "prospecting for a home."

The siege, 15–17 August 1782. Captain William Caldwell of Butler's Rangers, with the Indian Department agents Alexander McKee and the notorious Simon Girty, crossed the Ohio with about 50 rangers and some 300 Wyandot, Shawnee and Delaware warriors. Daniel Boone later guessed 400 to 500 in all. They surrounded the station before dawn, hoping to lure the garrison out. Inside were perhaps 90 people. The spring was outside the walls, and the fort needed water against fire arrows and thirst. So the women and girls, led (by one account) by Mary "Polly" Hawkins Craig, walked out with their buckets as if nothing were wrong, filled them in full view of the hidden warriors, and walked back. Not a shot was fired. Through the siege the attackers shot at the walls, burned crops and killed livestock. When word came that Kentucky militia were riding to the rescue, Caldwell pulled out early on 17 August, leaving a trail that was far too easy to follow. The 1896 Bryan Station memorial list of those "believed" to have been in the fort includes Barnett Rogers and Joseph Rogers.

Blue Licks, 19 August 1782. About 182 mounted militia gathered at Bryan's Station and chased the raiders northeast along the old buffalo trace to the salt springs at the Lower Blue Licks on the Licking River. Colonel John Todd had the command. Lieutenant Colonel Daniel Boone led the Fayette men, and Colonels Stephen Trigg and Hugh McGary the Lincoln County men. Colonel Benjamin Logan was a day behind with hundreds more. At the river, Boone, who knew the ground, warned that the open trail looked like an ambush and urged them to wait for Logan. Before the officers could agree, McGary spurred his horse into the ford with the shout remembered as "Them that ain't cowards, follow me!" and the men poured across after him.

On the ridge beyond, Caldwell's warriors were hidden in the ravines. The fight lasted perhaps fifteen minutes. The center and right broke within about five. Todd and Trigg were shot dead. Boone's son Israel, about 23, was shot through the neck at his father's side, and Boone had to leave his body and run for the ford. At the river Benjamin Netherland rallied a few men for a volley that checked the pursuit long enough for survivors to swim the Licking. Boone counted 77 Kentuckians killed and a dozen wounded, and several more were carried off as prisoners. About two of every five men who rode out never came home. Among the officers killed was "Lieutenant Barnett Rogers," our John's brother, named on the Blue Licks roll of honor alongside Col. John Todd, Col. Stephen Trigg and Maj. Silas Harlan.

Days later Logan arrived with about 460 men. With Boone they went back to the battlefield and buried the dead they could find in a common grave, by Boone's count 43 bodies; the rest were never found. The Rogers family history says Barnett's body was instead carried home and buried in the old Rogers graveyard at Bryan's Station, under a marked stone. Barnett had made his will two years earlier, in Culpeper, on 30 October 1780; it was proved there on 20 January 1783 and left his property to his brothers William and Joseph and his sisters.

The reckoning. In November 1782 George Rogers Clark led more than 1,000 Kentuckians, Logan and Boone among them, across the Ohio. They burned five Shawnee towns on the Great Miami, often called the last major American offensive of the Revolution. Blue Licks itself is remembered as the largest Revolutionary battle fought in Kentucky, and one of the last of the whole war.

A name to wonder about. Our Elizabeth Rogers was born about 1777 and, by family tradition, was a small girl inside Bryan's Station during the siege. She grew up as Elizabeth Todd Rogers. We have found nothing that explains the middle name. It is tempting to think she was named, or renamed, for Col. John Todd, who died at Blue Licks beside her uncle Barnett, but that is only a guess.

Joseph Hale stays. Joseph Hale Rogers never left. In June 1784 he took up his North Elkhorn land, which included Bryan's Station, and his family lived in some of the fort's old cabins. About 1796 he built a brick house there, added a second story in 1800, and ran his mills and still house on Elkhorn until he died on 13 July 1834 at about 92. He was buried in a walled lot in the old orchard. When the Daughters of the American Revolution built the stone wall around the Bryan Station spring in 1896, it stood near the old Rogers house.

If you want to visit. The Blue Licks Battlefield is now a Kentucky state resort park near Mount Olivet, with a monument and the mass grave on the ridge. The Bryan Station spring and its 1896 memorial wall are on Bryan Station Road on the northeast edge of Lexington.

Sources: Rogers family histories (c. 1920 and 1954); Courier-Journal, 19 Aug 1896; the Blue Licks roll of honor; Daniel Boone's letter of 30 Aug 1782 (as quoted by the Kentucky National Guard history); American Battlefield Trust pages on Bryan's Station and Blue Licks; Wikipedia's articles on Bryan Station and the Battle of Blue Licks. Numbers differ between sources; the ones above follow Boone where he gives them.

stories.title: Col. Charles W. Raphun (1842–1903)
stories.group: The Raphuns and the Blakelys (Emma Gordon's mother's mother's line)
stories.html:
Charles W. Raphun was born on 29 June 1842 in Philadelphia. In 1850 he was a boy of eight in Penn Township, Philadelphia. His father was dead by then, and his mother, Louisa (Blakely) Raphun, a Maryland woman, was listed separately in the city's Upper Delaware ward. By 1870 he had moved to his mother's city, Baltimore. In 1880 he was a clerk there, aged 37, with his wife Emma Sophia Boyd and their small children Charles M. and Edith B.

In June 1890 the special census of Union veterans and widows found him at 903 North Fulton Avenue, the same house where his aunt Kate was living in 1903. The census taker wrote his name and address but left his rank, regiment and dates blank.

He went to work in the U.S. Custom House at Baltimore and rose to deputy collector of customs for the Port of Baltimore. The newspapers called him "Col." Raphun. He died in Baltimore on 6 February 1903 and was buried at Woodlawn. Emma had died young, on 16 March 1888, and he married again, to Estelle V. McCreight.

stories.title: Kate (Blakely) Henderson (1816–?): the Colonel's aunt who knew Poe
stories.group: The Raphuns and the Blakelys (Emma Gordon's mother's mother's line)
stories.html:
The aunt and the poet. A month after the Colonel's death, on 2 March 1903, an old Baltimore lady named Mrs. Kate Henderson turned 87 at her home, 903 North Fulton Avenue. A reporter from the Baltimore Morning Herald came to see her, and the paper ran the story the next day under the headline "Was the Sweetheart of Edgar Allan Poe." It called her an aunt of the late Col. Charles W. Raphun.

Kate said she was born on 2 March 1816 in a house at the corner of Lombard Street and Marsh Market Space. She had lived in Baltimore all her life apart from a short stay in Philadelphia. She married three times, to a Mr. Payne, a Mr. Spangler and lastly a Mr. Henderson, who had died about forty years before. She had outlived all her children.

She told the reporter, modestly and only when pressed, that Poe had been an intimate friend. While he was a cadet at West Point (1830–31), he wrote her letters declaring his love and sent her little poems. A married daughter later took the letters to New Orleans, where they were treasured. After that daughter died, they were never found. According to the Poe Society's notes, Kate told a later paper that she had never really been Poe's sweetheart.

Poe in Baltimore. The dates fit Poe's life. He came to Baltimore in May 1829, just out of the army, poor and trying to publish his poems. His older brother Henry lived with their aunt, Maria Clemm. Poe went to Richmond early in 1830, and in June 1830 he entered West Point, giving a false age. He soon wanted out. In January 1831 he stopped going to formations and classes on purpose, was court-martialed on 28 January and dismissed. By May 1831 he was back in Baltimore, living with Mrs. Clemm, his bedridden grandmother, his little cousin Virginia (later his wife) and Henry, who died that August. Kate was 13 when Poe first came to Baltimore and 15 when he came back from West Point (American Heritage, "Cadet Edgar Allan Poe").

Why this fits our family. The paper never gave Kate's maiden name. The Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore, working only from her birth date and birthplace, identified her as Kate Bleakley/Blakely. Baltimore directories of 1822–23 list Matthew Blakeley, tavern keeper and grocer, at the corner of Water Street and Marsh Market Space, steps from where Kate said she was born. The Society did not know about our family. But the FamilySearch tree, made separately, gives Louisa Raphun's parents as Mathew Blakely and Ann Brown. So Kate and Louisa were very likely sisters, daughters of Matthew Blakely, and that is exactly why the paper called Kate the Colonel's aunt.

A Poe biographer knew her too. There is a third witness, independent of both. Hervey Allen's biography of Poe, Israfel (1926, revised 1934), names her. One of the first glimpses of Poe after he came back to Baltimore in 1831, Allen writes, is of him calling on "Kate Bleakely" in full cadet uniform, with his brother Henry. Allen says her father, Matthew Bleakley, kept the Armistead Hotel on Short Swan Street; that Kate was probably one of Henry's sweethearts; and that Poe later wrote verses to her (Israfel, ch. 15, pp. 258–259). Allen puts the visit after West Point, not during it, and says nothing about letters. So Kate's story of love letters from the Point may have grown a little over seventy years. But a Poe biographer knew of Poe calling on her, and knew her father was Matthew, which is the name the FamilySearch tree gives for Louisa's father.

How sure: the 1903 article and the 1880 census are records. Louisa's parents come from another tree, and Kate's maiden name is the Poe Society's inference. Two independent lines of evidence point to the same Blakely family, which makes it probable.
