stories.title: Corporal Charles B. Raphun (about 1816–1844)
stories.group: The Raphuns and the Blakelys (Emma Gordon's mother's mother's line)
stories.html:
The Colonel never knew his father. Charles B. Raphun, born in Philadelphia about 1816, married Louisa Blakely and had two sons, John Hancock and Charles W. He was a corporal in the National Greys, one of Philadelphia's volunteer militia companies. A notice headed "MILITARY FUNERAL" reported that "the funeral of Corporal Charles B. Raphun, of the National Greys, took place yesterday afternoon," and that he was "highly esteemed among the Greys, as a soldier." The FamilySearch tree gives his death as 2 August 1844.

The Kensington riots. That was the summer of Philadelphia's Nativist riots, also called the Bible riots. Native-born Protestants and the new Irish Catholic immigrants had been quarrelling over which Bible should be read in the public schools. On 3 May 1844 a Nativist (anti-immigrant) party held a rally in Kensington, the Irish mill district just north of the city, and was chased off. They came back on 6 May. It rained, the meeting crowded into a market house, and fighting spilled into the street. Shots came from nearby windows, and an 18-year-old Nativist, George Shiffler, was killed. Mobs then burned the Hibernia Hose House, about thirty Irish homes and the market. On 8 May they burned St. Michael's Church in Kensington and, that evening, St. Augustine's at Fourth and Vine. The mayor pleaded with them and was stoned, and the crowd cheered when the steeple fell.

On 7 May the sheriff called out the First Brigade of the Pennsylvania militia under Gen. George Cadwalader. These were volunteer companies like the Greys, ordinary working men who drilled in their spare time. The troops met little direct resistance, but they could not stop the fires. Calm came only around 10 May, after posses, police, militia from other cities and federal soldiers and sailors poured into the district (Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia; Wikipedia). Charles was on duty in Kensington in those days, and the Philadelphia Ledger's notice, reprinted in the Boston Messenger of 14 August 1844, says why he died three months later: "His death is attributed to fatigue and exposure while on duty during the riots in Kensington in May last." In July the violence broke out again in Southwark, where the militia fired cannon and muskets into the crowd and soldiers were killed. Whether Charles was well enough to turn out again in July is not known.

He was also a member of the Perseverance Hose Company, a volunteer fire company. At his funeral the National Greys under Capt. P. Fritz and the City Guards under Capt. Hill formed the military escort, with a band playing martial music. His fellow firemen walked four abreast ahead of the hearse, and the family followed in carriages. He was buried at Monument Cemetery "in a becoming and creditable manner." His son Charles was two years old.

A slip kept with the burial papers gives the medical side plainly: "Chas Raphun expired August 2nd 1844 of Tubercular Phthisis", aged 28, with "Monument Cemetery" written on the back. Phthisis was tuberculosis, the "consumption" of the time. That fits both his age (born about 1816) and the newspaper's "fatigue and exposure": a man already sick with TB, standing guard in the rain through the riots, could easily have gone downhill over the summer.

The name. The family tree on FamilySearch carries the name back through John Raphun (1772–1825) of Philadelphia to a Johann Bernhardt Rebhuhn. Rebhuhn is German for "partridge". That line is only in other people's trees so far.

stories.title: The Boyds
stories.group: The Raphuns and the Blakelys (Emma Gordon's mother's mother's line)
stories.html:
Emma Raphun's father, Francis H. B. "Frank" Boyd, was a Baltimore carpenter and builder, and by the end of his life a "measurer, surveyor and adjuster" of buildings. He was a Past Grand of the Golden Rule Lodge No. 58 of the Odd Fellows. In the Civil War draft of 1865 he was called up and furnished a substitute, paying another man to serve in his place, which was legal then. It was common among men who could afford it, and Frank was about 44 with a family to keep. Substitute brokers advertised in Maryland papers. In January 1865 one, Howard & Co., promised drafted men a substitute "on the most reasonable terms" without their having to come into Baltimore (Frederick Examiner, 11 Jan 1865). Even in 1862 a substitute in Baltimore cost $150 to $400 (Valley Register, 24 Oct 1862), and prices climbed as the war went on. He died of liver disease after a long illness on 16 May 1875 at his home, 176 Townsend Street, and was buried in Greenmount Cemetery, "in the 55th year of his age" (Baltimore American). His wife, Sarah Ann (Hopkins) Boyd, outlived him by 35 years. She died in Washington, D.C., at 1516 R Street, aged 86, on 15 January 1910 and was brought home to Baltimore for burial. Frank's father was probably Joseph Boyd, a Baltimore hatter born in 1789, who married Mary Hiner in 1811.

The substitute. The enlistment paper for Frank's substitute survives. Frank was drafted on 30 March 1865 in the 5th sub-district of Maryland's 2nd District. On 11 April 1865 a man named John Robinson, born in Ireland, aged 24, a laborer, five feet eleven, with grey eyes, brown hair and a fair complexion, signed with his mark to serve three years in Frank's place "for a sufficient consideration paid." Lee had surrendered at Appomattox two days earlier, so the war was all but over, and Robinson probably never fired a shot.

A guardian's bond, 1853. In March 1853 the Orphans' Court of Baltimore County made Joseph C. Boyd guardian of three orphaned boys, John K., Richard and Joseph Jorden, sons of the late John M. Jorden. Joseph's two sureties were Henry Brackin and Francis H. B. Boyd. Frank's middle names were "H. B.", and the B. was Bracken, so Henry Brackin was very likely a relative on his mother's side, and Joseph C. Boyd perhaps a brother. Neither link is proven yet.

Frank's will. Frank's will was proved on 22 May 1875, six days after his death, and recorded in Baltimore City Wills, Liber J.H.B. No. 41, folio 393. His widow Sarah A. Boyd got a third of his personal property outright and a third of his real estate for life. The rest was split three ways. His daughters Emma S. Raphun and Charlotte V. Boyd each got a third for life, "for her sole and separate use", which kept it out of a husband's hands, and then to her children. The last third did not go straight to his son Francis H. B. Boyd Jr. It went to two trustees, Hugh B. Jones and John T. Morris, who were to invest it and pay the son the income in quarterly instalments "for his personal maintenance and support." The son could not borrow against the payments, sell them or mortgage them, and whatever he already owed his father "on my books" was to be taken out of his share and given to his sisters. A father does not write a clause like that for a son he trusts with money. The witnesses were Benjamin Kurtz, Arthur L. Spamer and C. Augustus E. Spamer, and the Orphans' Court admitted the will on 26 May 1875.

Sources: Substitute Volunteer Enlistment no. 39, 2nd District of Maryland, 11 Apr 1865; Baltimore County Orphans' Court proceedings, March 1853, p. 93; will of Francis H. B. Boyd, Baltimore City Register of Wills, 1875 (original papers and Liber J.H.B. 41, f. 393).

Sources: 1850, 1860, 1870 and 1880 censuses (indexes); Edith B. Callahan's Maryland death record; Baltimore Morning Herald, 3 Mar 1903, p. 12, transcribed by the Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore; Washington Times, 3 Mar 1903; 1844 funeral notice (OldNews obituary index); Baltimore American, 18 May 1875; D.C. deaths index, 1910.

stories.title: Edward J. Callahan and Edith Raphun
stories.group: The Callahans and the Rooneys (Emma Gordon's mother's father's line)
stories.html: The Colonel's daughter Edith Blakely Raphun was born in Baltimore on 29 September 1879. She married Edward J. Callahan, a Baltimore man born on 9 April 1875. Their wedding notice tells a lot in a few lines. They were married "in the presence of a few friends" on a Tuesday afternoon in the parsonage of St. Martin's Catholic Church, Fulton Avenue and Fayette Street. The bride was the daughter of Mr. C. W. Raphun, deputy collector of customs, "who lives at 903 North Fulton avenue", which is the same house where old Kate Henderson, the Colonel's aunt who remembered Poe, was living in 1903. So Kate spent her last years with her nephew's family. Edith wore "a traveling dress of brown broadcloth, with hat and gloves to match", and the couple left at once for a trip South. Edward was "a prominent member of the Ariel Boat Club", one of Baltimore's rowing clubs, and had rowed in the "Ariel Four", which "won a number of victories". On their return they lived at 1622 West Lanvale Street, his family's house. In 1910 they were in Ward 15 with Edward Jr., Edith R. and little Emma Louise, born 8 April 1904. Rosalie and Charles Leland (born 2 February 1914) followed. Emma Louise married William Charles Gordon at Ellicott City on 20 July 1922, and they were Michael's great-grandparents. Edward died on 15 February 1950 and is buried at Lorraine Park Cemetery. Edith Callahan lived to 86 and died at Towson on 11 April 1966. (Her headstone gives her birthday as 28 September 1879.)

stories.title: William O. Callahan (about 1840–1892)
stories.group: The Callahans and the Rooneys (Emma Gordon's mother's father's line)
stories.html:
Edward's father, William O. Callahan, was born about 1840. The 1880 census says Ireland; the tree says Staten Island, but that place comes from his son's New York birth record, which gives where the family lived, not where William was born. The working tree attaches U.S. Navy enlistment records from Baltimore in August 1864, in the last year of the Civil War. They have not been read yet.

He married Frances Rooney. Their son William was born in New York City on 11 February 1873, and by 1880 the family was in Baltimore with Edward, Mary, William and Charley. Later came May, Frank and Carmelite. William died at home, 1622 West Lanvale Street, on 21 November 1892, aged about 52 (Baltimore American, 24 Nov 1892). Frances outlived him by almost forty years and died in Baltimore on 5 February 1931.

stories.title: Frances Rooney (1852–1931): a girl from the frontier
stories.group: The Callahans and the Rooneys (Emma Gordon's mother's father's line)
stories.html:
A girl from the Kansas frontier. Every record has Frances born in Kansas, on 7 July 1852. That is strange, because Kansas Territory was not created until 1854. In 1852 the area was Indian country, and the main white settlement was the army post at Fort Leavenworth. The working tree shows Frances in Leavenworth in 1865, and her mother, Margaret (Carr) Rooney, a Philadelphian born about 1828, dying there about 1864. If that is right, Frances was born at or near the fort, perhaps to a soldier's family, before Kansas existed. Her father is named only as Thomas Rooney. The 1865 Kansas state census has now answered that.

Probably born in Indiana after all. The 1860 census of the Rooney household in Leavenworth lists no Frances, but it does list a daughter Sarah, 8, born in Indiana, the right age to be her. Five years later the 1865 Kansas census lists Frances, 13, and no Sarah, though it gives her birthplace as Missouri. Sarah and Frances look like the same girl, perhaps a Sarah Frances who went by her middle name. The family's path fits it: Mary was born in Kentucky about 1850, Sarah in Indiana about 1852, Emma in Kentucky about 1854 and Eliza in Ohio about 1856, before they reached Kansas. Her later records probably said Kansas because that is where she grew up.

stories.title: Thomas Rooney (about 1821–1887): baker and soldier at Fort Leavenworth
stories.group: The Callahans and the Rooneys (Emma Gordon's mother's father's line)
stories.html:
Thomas Rooney, baker and soldier. In the 1865 Kansas census at Leavenworth, Frances, 13 (born in Missouri), is living with her father, Thos. Rooney, 44, born in Ireland, and her younger sister and brother, Elizabeth, 9 (born in Ohio), and Edward, 7 (born in Kansas). The children's birthplaces in the 1860 census map the family's travels: Mary in Kentucky about 1850, Sarah in Indiana about 1852, Emma J. in Kentucky about 1854, Eliza in Ohio about 1856 and John E. in Missouri about 1858. That is the moving life of a soldier's family. (Sarah, aged 8 and born about 1852, may be Frances under another name.) In that 1860 Leavenworth census, Thomas, 42, was there with his wife Margaret, 32, born in Pennsylvania, and children Mary, Sarah, Emma J., Eliza and John E. (Frances isn't listed under that name, which needs a look at the page.) "Missouri" for Frances makes sense: the fort sits on the Kansas side of the Missouri River, and Missouri was the settled side in 1852.

The best record of Thomas is the register of the National Home for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers at Leavenworth, which took him in as an old man. It says he was born in Ireland, was 66 in 1885, a baker, a Catholic and a widower. He enlisted at Fort Leavenworth on 31 August 1861 in Company A, 8th Kansas Infantry, at about 42, and was discharged on 30 August 1864, at the end of his three years. The clerk added a line that explains how the family came to be on the frontier at all: he "was also in the Mexican War" (1846–48). An Irishman who had been a soldier in Mexico, living by the army's great western fort, fits a man who came west with the army and stayed.

Company A spent its first eighteen months on the frontier and the Missouri border: a march to West Point, Missouri, in December 1861; garrison duty at Fort Kearney, Nebraska, on the Oregon Trail, from February to June 1862; then Leavenworth, with skirmishes against Confederate guerrillas at Hickory Grove, Missouri, in August 1862. In February 1863 the company joined the rest of the regiment at Nashville, and the 8th Kansas fought at Chickamauga in September 1863 and in the storming of Missionary Ridge in November (8th Kansas Infantry). Whether Thomas, then in his forties, marched with them or stayed on detached duty, his service record would show. Margaret died at Leavenworth about 1864, while he was away at war or just home from it.

Thomas died at the soldiers' home on 25 September 1887. His government headstone reads "Co A 8 Regt Kan Inf". The register named his nearest relative as his son John E. Rooney of Davenport, Iowa; Frances was by then a wife and mother in Baltimore.

Growing up at the edge of the West. In 1852 Fort Leavenworth, founded in 1827 on the bluffs of the Missouri, was the army's jumping-off point for the plains. Its soldiers escorted wagon trains on the Santa Fe and Oregon trails. There was no town yet. The town of Leavenworth was laid out in June 1854, just after the Kansas-Nebraska Act opened the territory, and held its first lot sale that October. Frances grew up through "Bleeding Kansas", when the army at the fort tried to keep the peace between pro-slavery and free-state settlers, and through the Civil War, when thousands of volunteers were mustered at the fort and Leavenworth became the largest town in Kansas, with about 20,000 people by 1865. Her mother died there about 1864, the year Confederate General Sterling Price marched toward the fort and was beaten at Westport, Missouri, in October (Kansas Historical Society; Legends of America).

Sources: 1880, 1900, 1910 and 1920 censuses (indexes); New York City birth index, 1873; Maryland marriage index, 1922; Edith Callahan's death record; Baltimore American, 24 Nov 1892 (obituary index); FamilySearch tree for Frances and Margaret (Carr) Rooney.

stories.title: William Charles Gordon (1900–1989), two-war veteran
stories.group: The Gordons and the Deveneys (Emma Gordon's father's line)
stories.html: William Charles Gordon was born in Baltimore on 10 April 1900. His veteran's marker sums up his service: "Pvt US Marine Corps, Pvt US Army, World War I & II." He was a Marine at the very end of the First World War (November 1918 to March 1919), and again in the Second, from August 1943 to May 1944, when he was 43. Between the wars he married Emma Louise Callahan (1922), and their daughter Emma Louise Gordon, Michael's grandmother, was born on 23 September 1927. In the 1940s he lived at 603 Ingleside Avenue, Catonsville. He died on 29 July 1989 and lies in Garrison Forest Veterans Cemetery, Owings Mills.

stories.title: William Gordon (1868–1941), from Chicago
stories.group: The Gordons and the Deveneys (Emma Gordon's father's line)
stories.html:
His father, also William Gordon, was born in Chicago on 8 June 1868, according to his son's birth record and his own death record. How a Chicago boy came to Baltimore is not yet known.

The fish man. William made his living from the Chesapeake. Kristin found him in the census as the owner of his own fish business, a fish distribution company, and a Baltimore city directory lists him as "pres Gordon & Co Inc", living at 3704 Copley Road. The business was Gordon & Co. In his day nearly all of Baltimore's fish came through one place: the wholesale Fish Market on Market Place, by the harbor, built in 1907 after the Great Fire of 1904 had destroyed the old market hall. It was one of three market buildings in a row on the site of the old Centre ("Marsh") Market, where fish had been sold since the 1770s, and it stayed Baltimore's wholesale fish market until 1984. The building is now the Port Discovery children's museum (Historical Marker Database; Baltimore Heritage). A dealer like William would have bought from the boats and watermen before dawn and sold on to the city's retail stalls, grocers and restaurants. We don't know yet whether Gordon & Co. had a stand in that market or its own premises. Baltimore city directories of the 1900s–1930s, which list fish dealers by name and address, and Baltimore Sun business notices should tell us. He married Annie Louretta Deveney and raised William, Anna Lauretta, Bernard Norris and Lawrence. In 1930–40 the family lived at 3704 Copley Road. William died at Catonsville on 1 August 1941. His parents are unknown. (The working tree attaches a Massachusetts marriage of a different William Gordon, which is not him.)

stories.title: Michael Deveney (died 1899)
stories.group: The Gordons and the Deveneys (Emma Gordon's father's line)
stories.html: Annie's father, Michael Deveney, was born in Ireland, about 1834 by one record and about 1850 by another. He died on 24 February 1899 at his home, 418½ North High Street, "beloved husband of Bridget Deveney", and his Requiem Mass was at St. Vincent de Paul's, the old Irish parish near the Jones Falls.

stories.title: Bridget (Burke) Deveney (1858–1929): from Rochdale to Baltimore, and the Grogans of Lancashire
stories.group: The Gordons and the Deveneys (Emma Gordon's father's line)
stories.html:
His wife Bridget was born in England on 13 February 1858, to an Irish mother whose death record names only as "E. Grogan". She lived until 21 March 1929 and was buried in St. Vincent's Cemetery. In 1870, aged about 13, she was in Baltimore as "Bridget Burk".

The tree linked her to Lawrence and Bridget Grogan, Irish-born. In 1861 they lived at 6 Richard Street, Castleton, near Rochdale in Lancashire, a mill district full of Irish families who had left after the Famine. By 1870 they were in Baltimore, where Lawrence died on 8 January 1878. Another tree gives his birthplace as "Boffin Island", Galway, which is probably Inishbofin, an island off the Galway coast. Their 1861 children were Thomas, Bridget, Peter and Ann, but their Bridget was 21, far too old to be ours.

Our Bridget turns up just down the street, as a Burke. The same census taker, on the same page, found the household of Honor Burke on Rose Street, Castleton, nineteen households before the Grogans. Honor was a widow of 58, born in Ireland, "formerly house keeper". With her were her daughter Winniford, 20, her son Francis Burke, 32, a coal fitter, unmarried, both born in Ireland, and two children born in Rochdale: Michael Burke, 6, and Bridget Burke, 4. The census taker wrote the children down as Honor's son and daughter, but a woman of 58 does not have a four-year-old, so they were almost certainly her grandchildren. Bridget's age fits her birth in 1857 or 1858. Her brother explains the voyage: on 5 September 1868 Michael Burke, 14, and Bridget Burke, 11, landed at Baltimore on the steamer Carroll from Liverpool. Two years later she was "Bridget Burk", 13, in Baltimore.

So she was a Burke by birth and a Grogan through her mother, the "E. Grogan" of her death record. E. was probably an older daughter of Lawrence and Bridget, and she was in neither household in 1861. Francis may have been the children's father (the census calls him single, which may be wrong) or their uncle; that is still open.

Inishbofin is now confirmed. When Bridget Grogan died on 20 May 1887, aged 75, the Baltimore Sun called her "relict of the late Laurence Grogan, a native of Inishbofin, county Galway, Ireland", and her funeral went from her home on East Hoffman Street to St. Vincent's Church. Lawrence's own headstone at St. Vincent de Paul's cemetery calls him a native of "Boffin Island", aged 68, and also remembers their son Thomas.

Sources: Maryland birth and death indexes; Social Security application; VA benefit and burial records; Baltimore death notice, 27 Feb 1899; 1861 England census and 1870 U.S. census (indexes); Bridget Deveney's death index.

stories.title: John Karmann (1856–1939) and Anna Weber
stories.group: The Karmanns: from Vienna to a Baltimore drugstore (George Karman's father's line)
stories.html:
The Karman name came from Vienna. John Karmann was born there on 28 September 1856, the son of Joseph Karmann and Margaret Stacker, both Viennese, according to his 1939 Maryland death record. Every census calls him Austrian.

In Baltimore he married Anna E. Weber, who was about nine years older than he was. The 1900 census gives her birth as December 1847 in Denmark; later censuses say Germany. Their children were Frank (about 1876), Lizzie (1887), George (1890 or 1891) and Anna E. (1894 or 1895). The family lived in Ward 8 of Baltimore in 1910 and were still in the city in 1930. John died in Baltimore on 8 February 1939, aged 82.

An iron worker. John's death certificate (Baltimore No. 54944) shows how he made his living: he was an iron worker for the Bethlehem company, Bethlehem Steel, which ran the huge Sparrows Point steel works and shipyards at Baltimore, and he last worked in 1924, at about 68. That fits the family memory that the Austrian Karmanns were blacksmiths. The certificate also confirms his birth in Vienna on 28 September 1856 and names his parents, Joseph Karmann and Margaret Stacker, both of Vienna. He and Anna lived at 1714 East Oliver Street in East Baltimore, where Anna Emilie Karmann, "née Weber", died on 9 March 1933. Her funeral was at Trinity Lutheran Church, McElderry and Port Streets, and both were buried in Baltimore Cemetery.

German Baltimore. The Karmanns lived their lives in Baltimore's large German community. In October 1895 the city's German daily, Der Deutsche Correspondent, reported a new lodge of the Independent Order of Heptasophs, a fraternal insurance society, with John Karmann on its finance committee. In January 1897 the same paper listed an "Anna Karmann" among six flag maidens at the dedication of a new flag for a brewers' and coopers' union. Flag maidens were usually young women, so this may be a relative rather than John's wife.

Where was Anna from? The records disagree. The 1900 census says Denmark, December 1847; later censuses say Germany (the 1910 census gives her age as 62, against John's 53). Family trees give 21 December 1857 in Copenhagen, with parents Johann Heinrich Weber and Emma Johanne Dorothee Saeger, but attach a baptism of 11 March 1849 at Versmold in Westphalia. The 1857 date doesn't fit the censuses, which make her about nine years older than John. Her own death certificate (1933) should help.

stories.title: George Karmann (1891–1976), druggist
stories.group: The Karmanns: from Vienna to a Baltimore drugstore (George Karman's father's line)
stories.html:
George Karmann was born in Baltimore on 20 September 1891 (his draft card; other records say 1890). He became a druggist, and the 1927 city directory lists him as one. His name turns up in Baltimore's German-language daily, Der Deutsche Correspondent, in September 1912.

A pharmacy student who wrote for the college paper. George trained at the University of Maryland's school of pharmacy in Baltimore, class of 1916. In the University Gazette, the university's monthly journal, he is listed among the undergraduate members of the editorial board on 1 December 1915 ("George Karmann, '16 ... Pharmacy"), and by 1 March 1916 he was on the editorial staff as the pharmacy school's representative.

Buying and selling land. Baltimore's real-estate transfers, printed in Der Deutsche Correspondent on 23 September 1917, show George Karmann and his wife selling a lot on the west side of Montford Avenue near Hoffman Street, 15 by 70 feet, to Caroline E. Lowe. Five years later the Annapolis Evening Capital (8 July 1922) reported a deed from David Scarlett Ross to George Karmann and wife for a tract of land called "Riverdale" in Anne Arundel County, likely a place on the water outside the city.

Sources: University Gazette (University of Maryland, Baltimore), 1 Dec 1915 p. 92 and 1 Mar 1916 p. 151; Der Deutsche Correspondent, 23 Sep 1917, p. 7; Evening Capital and Maryland Gazette, 8 Jul 1922, p. 4.

He married Irene Emma Korpman, a Baltimore girl born on 10 February 1891, and their children were Grace, Irene Emily (born 16 December 1914), Annie (later Beatrice) and George Jr. (born 10 May 1927). In the late 1920s and 1930s the family lived at 3112 and then 3214 Juneau Place, and in 1942 at 2541 Pickwick Road. Somewhere along the way the second "n" fell away, and the census taker of 1930 even wrote "Kormann".

In later life George and Irene moved to Southern California, as their son did. Irene died on 6 October 1975 and George on 12 April 1976. They share a headstone at Green Hills Memorial Park, Rancho Palos Verdes: "George, Sept. 20, 1890 – Apr. 12, 1976; Irene E., Feb. 10, 1891 – Oct. 6, 1975." (The stone says 1890; his own draft card says 1891.)

stories.title: George J. Karman Jr. (1927–1993)
stories.group: The Karmanns: from Vienna to a Baltimore drugstore (George Karman's father's line)
stories.html:
George Karman Jr. served in the military from July 1945 to August 1947. He married Emma Louise Gordon, and they raised their sons in Baltimore, among them Michael's father. They later moved to Huntington Beach, California, where George died on 18 June 1993 and Emma on 17 June 1999.

Sources: 1900, 1910, 1930 censuses; John Karmann's Maryland death record; WWII draft registration (1942); Baltimore city directories; Irene E. Karmann's 1914 birth record; California death index; BillionGraves; VA claims index; Social Security application; Social Security NUMIDENT file for George Karmann Jr. (born 10 May 1927, Baltimore; applied June 1943; died 18 June 1993; parents George Karmann and Irene Korpmann).

stories.title: Family tradition: the Karmann Ghia cousin
stories.group: The Karmanns: from Vienna to a Baltimore drugstore (George Karman's father's line)
stories.html:
The family tells that, generations ago, a distant cousin asked one of the Karman grandfathers for money to start a car company. He said no, and the company became the maker of the Karmann Ghia. A second story says that when Kristin's father-in-law tried to trace this side in the 1990s, he got a cease-and-desist letter.

What the records say so far:

  • The firm was Wilhelm Karmann GmbH of Osnabrück. Its founder, Wilhelm Karmann Sr., was born on 14 February 1871 at Ilfeld in the Harz. He was the son of August Karmann, a wheelwright in Krefeld, and was a Catholic. His biography notes that the family name had earlier been spelled "Karman".
  • In 1901 he took over an existing Osnabrück carriage-building shop. He built his first car body in 1902. How he paid for the shop isn't recorded. In 1924 he made a trip to the United States to study production methods.
  • The Karmann Ghia is one model (a body style), not the company. Karmann built it from 1955, under Wilhelm Jr., with a design by Ghia of Turin on a Volkswagen chassis. By then the Karmann coachworks had been building car bodies for over fifty years.

Family memory also says the first Karmanns who came from Austria worked as blacksmiths. If so, they were in the same family of trades as Wilhelm's father, a wheelwright, and Wilhelm himself, who built carriages. That is a coincidence of craft, not proof of kinship. John Karmann's death certificate calls him an iron worker for Bethlehem Steel, so he did work with iron; the 1900 and 1910 censuses may show whether he started as a smith.

So the only time a cousin could have asked for start-up money was around 1901. The man asked would have been John Karmann (1856–1939) in Baltimore, or someone in his generation. The fit isn't obvious: John's family was Viennese and Wilhelm's was from the Rhineland. A link through the Karman/Karmann name is possible but unproven. Wilhelm's 1924 American trip is worth noting in case he visited relatives.

How sure: family tradition only. No record yet connects the Baltimore Karmanns to Wilhelm Karmann. Tests: John's 1856 Vienna baptism and his father Joseph's origins, compared with Wilhelm's Krefeld ancestry; a Karman-surname Y-DNA test against a Karmann descendant; any surviving family letters.
stories.quest: The family tradition of a Karmann cousin and a famous car

stories.title: Lorenz Korpman (1832–?), from Bad Dürkheim to the Union cavalry
stories.group: The Korpmans, Ecks and Wempes (George Karman's mother's line)
stories.html:
Irene Korpman's grandfather was christened Lorenz Korbmann on 24 January 1832 in the Reformed church at Bad Dürkheim, a wine town in the Palatinate, then part of Bavaria. His parents, Johann Lorenz Korbmann and Friderika Elisabetha Körber, had married in the same church on 10 March 1825. Johann Lorenz came from Merchingen in Baden, where he was christened in 1790, the son of Martin and Eva Korbmann. Friderika was a Dürkheim girl, born in 1792 and buried there in 1854.

Lorenz sailed for New York in 1854, at about 22, and was naturalized there. By the early 1860s he was in Baltimore, where his son Albert Adam was born on 12 February 1863. That summer the Union army began raising the 3rd Maryland Cavalry, the "Bradford Dragoons", in Baltimore. The state's roster of Maryland volunteers lists "Korbman, Lorenz", private, Company C, enlisted 16 July 1863 (History and Roster of Maryland Volunteers, p. 764). Company C was one of four companies raised in Baltimore City. Four others were filled with Confederate prisoners from Fort Delaware who had taken the oath of allegiance, so Lorenz's regiment had former rebels in its ranks.

A short war. The roster ends Lorenz's service in two words: "Deserted, September 14, 1863." He had been in uniform two months. The regiment was still on duty in the defenses of Baltimore, and he had a wife and a baby of seven months at home. He was far from alone: the roster of the 3rd Maryland Cavalry is thick with men marked "Deserted", most of them in the first months. Some deserters had taken an enlistment bounty and gone; some had families who could not live on a private's pay; and some "desertions" were paperwork errors put right later. Lorenz's own service record at the National Archives would tell which.

The war he left was a hard one. In January 1864 the regiment shipped to Louisiana. It fought in the bayou country during the failed Red River campaign, at Mansura, Marksville and Yellow Bayou in May 1864. In August it sailed to Mobile Bay and helped besiege and capture Fort Morgan, and it ended the war in the Mobile campaign at Spanish Fort and Fort Blakely. Its quartermaster drowned near Morganza, Louisiana; men were lost at sea on the transport North America; one was shot by firing squad. Disease killed 84 of the regiment, against 11 who died of wounds. It was mustered out at Vicksburg on 7 September 1865 (regimental history).

Later Lorenz took his family to Buffalo, New York, where he worked as a gardener. In June 1876 a fire destroyed his one-story frame house at 57 "Lauret" (probably Laurel) Street; the family's belongings were saved. By 1880 they were back in Baltimore, the census taker writing the name "Corbman".

stories.title: Delone Eck and her parents, Christopher and Elizabeth
stories.group: The Korpmans, Ecks and Wempes (George Karman's mother's line)
stories.html:
Lorenz's wife, Delone ("Lena") Eck, was born on 28 May 1843. In 1851, aged eight, she landed at Baltimore on the ship Anna with her father, Christoph Eck, a shoemaker of about 45, from Eisenach. She later married a Mr. Davis and died at Towson on 24 November 1928.

Christopher and Elizabeth (Zimmermann) Eck settled first in Baltimore County, then in the hills of Harford County near the Rocks of Deer Creek. A daughter born in Germany on 3 February 1851, just before they sailed, was named America. In 1868 Christopher and Elizabeth, with Gotlieb and Wilhelmina Eck (probably a son and his wife), signed a deed to Samuel Johnson for land near Hanway's Mill. Hard times followed: the property went to a constable's sale in 1872 and a trustee's sale in 1879. Christopher died in April 1885, aged 79, and was buried at Cooptown.

Elizabeth lived another eleven years. The Aegis & Intelligencer reported that she died at the home of Dennis Knopp (America's husband), near the Rocks, "in the 87th year of her age", leaving 6 children and 47 grandchildren, and was buried at Cooptown Methodist church. The tree says she was born in Kusel, in the Palatinate. That doesn't sit easily with Eisenach, which is in Thuringia. See the open questions.

stories.title: Albert Korpman and the Wempes
stories.group: The Korpmans, Ecks and Wempes (George Karman's mother's line)
stories.html:
Albert A. Korpman (1863–1940) was a brewer in 1888 and later a butcher, in the Gardenville district just outside Baltimore. He married Emma Florence Wempe, and their children included Albert, Mary, Irene, Harry, Walter, Edith and Grace.

Emma's father, Henry Wempe, came from Oldenburg. A passenger list shows an Engel Wempe, born about 1779, arriving at Baltimore in 1838–39, the year the tree has Henry arriving, so she may have been his mother. In 1880 Henry was farming at Gardenville with his wife Sarah Louisa and six children. He died about 1882, and the court granted his widow letters to settle his estate. Sarah Louisa died on 6 July 1901, aged 70, and her funeral was at St. James' Church.

Sources: Germany births and marriages indexes (Bad Dürkheim 1825, 1832; Merchingen 1790); New York passenger and naturalization indexes; U.S. Civil War soldiers index; 3rd Maryland Cavalry history; Buffalo Evening Republic, 2 Jun 1876; 1860–1880 censuses; Baltimore passenger card index, 1851; Albert Korpman's and Delona Davis's Maryland death records; Harford Co. sale notices, 1872 and 1879; Aegis & Intelligencer, 10 Apr 1896; Sarah L. Wempe obituary index, 1901.

stories.title: Three George Washington Carters
stories.group: The Carters and Rollisons of Kent County (George W. Carter III's father's line)
stories.html:
The Carter side has three men in a row named George Washington Carter, which the records sort out by suffix.

  • George W. Carter Sr. was born about October 1853 in Queen Anne's County. In 1880 he was farming at Church Hill with his wife Sarah Catherine "Kate" Rollison and six children: Charles, Lillie, Katie, Levin Ludlow, David and George W. Jr. Kate, born in Chestertown on 10 July 1851, was the daughter of Levin Ludlow Rollison and Martha Rawleigh. She lived to 89 and died at her son Julian R. Carter's home on High Street, Chestertown, on 18 February 1941. Her death certificate names her parents as Leven L. Rollison and Martha Gordon (the family tree said Martha Rawleigh; we are going with the certificate). Her father, Levin Ludlow Rollison, died on Monday 10 April 1871, aged 52 years, 3 months and 2 days, leaving a widow and nine children (Kent News, 22 April 1871). A War of 1812 index card names a Levin Rolason (filed also as "Roleison"), corporal and private in the 21st (Reed's) Regiment, Maryland Militia. That was the Kent County regiment that, under Lt. Col. Philip Reed, beat off a night raid by British sailors and marines at Caulk's Field on 31 August 1814, killing their commander, Sir Peter Parker of HMS Menelaus; the British lost 14 killed and 27 wounded, the militia had three wounded (National Park Service). Our Levin Ludlow was born about 1819, so the 1812 soldier was most likely his father, an older Levin (Find a Grave calls ours "Levin Ludlow Rollison Jr."). Whether that Levin was at Caulk's Field that night is not yet shown; the militia service record would say.
  • George W. Carter Jr. was born in Kent County on 5 October 1874. He married Nettie Mae Passwaters and lived at Worton in 1910 and 1930. They had at least nine children: Margaret, Norman, Lola, Pauline, Cartenne, Martha, Evelyn, Audrey and George III. He died suddenly at home on 11 October 1932, aged 58, and is buried in Chester Cemetery, Chestertown. A Delaware paper, the Smyrna Times, headed its notice "Passes Away Near Chestertown" and called him a "former sheriff of Kent county." Both 1932 notices call him "former Sheriff", so the family memory is solid. The official list of Kent County sheriffs we checked has no Carter in his lifetime, so either the list is incomplete or he served as a deputy or acting sheriff. Kent County court records or the Kent News should say which.

Father and son in the same fortnight. George Jr. died suddenly on Tuesday, 11 October 1932, after a "paralytic stroke", and was buried in Chester Cemetery after a funeral at the house. The Smyrna Times notice says he was "survived by his parents, his widow," and seven children: Mrs. Harold Williams, Mrs. Harvey Smith, Mrs. James E. Smith, Mrs. Edward Robinson, Miss Elizabeth Carter, George Carter 3rd and Norman Carter. A week later the paper ran a second notice, headed "Follows Son in Death After Week": his father, Geo. W. Carter, 81, a former employee of the Maryland State Roads Commission, "died early Thursday at his home in Chestertown" (Thursday 20 October 1932), leaving four daughters, six sons and his wife. He was buried in Chester Cemetery too, under a stone reading "George W. Carter Sr. 1852 — 1932". (Find a Grave's date of 12 October for him is wrong.) Kate Carter buried a son and a husband in ten days, and lived nine more years. - George W. Carter III, Michael's grandfather, was born at Fairlee, Kent County, on 17 September 1916. His grave marker shows he served in the Second World War as a captain in the U.S. Army. He married Elise Rebecca Glanding of Caroline County. She was still single in July 1940, when the Queen Anne's Record Observer reported "Miss Elise Glanding" spending a Sunday at Tolchester beach with her married sister, Mrs. Roy Cronshaw. In 1950 they lived on Queen Street, Chestertown. In August 1957 the same paper listed "Mr. and Mrs. Geo. Carter and their children" at a large family gathering. He died in Chestertown on 6 May 1985. Elise lived to 91 and died at Winfield, Carroll County, on 1 February 2010.

Levin Ludlow Rollison's estate took nine years to settle. The Kent County inventory was taken in 1871 and the first account passed on 7 May 1872. On 18 February 1880 his widow Martha E. signed away her right to administer it at Crumpton, and a new bond was posted on 2 March. One puzzle remains: when their son Levin L. Rollison died in Wilmington in 1936, his death record named his mother as "Martha Frazer", not Gordon.

Above George Sr., the working tree carries the Carters and Rollisons back to the colonial Eastern Shore, but almost none of it has sources yet.

Sources: 1880, 1910, 1920, 1930, 1950 censuses; George W. Carter III's Maryland birth and death records; Smyrna Times, 19 Oct 1932 (obituary index); Queen Anne's Record Observer, 1940 and 8 Aug 1957; Kent County sheriffs list; FamilySearch tree for Kate Rollison.

stories.title: James E. Passwaters (1844–1921), Union soldier
stories.group: The Passwaters, Adamses, Glandings and Hunters (the Eastern Shore lines)
stories.html:
James Edward Passwaters was born on 7 February 1844 in Nanticoke Hundred, Sussex County, Delaware, the son of William B. Passwaters and his wife Nancy. In 1850 he was six, living in Sussex County with his mother and his brothers and sister.

In the Civil War he served in the 6th Delaware Infantry, a short-term Union regiment. Its men drilled at home through the winter of 1862–63 and went on active duty in late June 1863, just as Lee's army crossed into Pennsylvania. They guarded the Philadelphia, Wilmington and Baltimore Railroad and its bridges near Havre de Grace and the Susquehanna, and some guarded Confederate prisoners at Fort Delaware. The regiment went home in August and September 1863. James was listed again as a veteran in 1890.

He married Margaret Ellen Adams, born in Delaware on 12 February 1838, daughter of Henry Fisher Adams and Margaret Ross. Her father died in 1843, when she was five. In 1880 James was farming at Greensborough, Caroline County, Maryland, with Margaret, their sons James, William, Charles and George, little Nettie, and his old father William. He died at Ridgely on 26 October 1921, aged 77 years, 8 months and 19 days, and his death certificate names his father "Wm. B. Passwaters" and his wife "Maggie E." Margaret died in May 1927.

stories.title: George W. Glanding and Wilhelmina Carter of Queen Anne's County
stories.group: The Passwaters, Adamses, Glandings and Hunters (the Eastern Shore lines)
stories.html: George W. Glanding, born about 1830, was in the First Election District of Queen Anne's County in 1860. By 1870 he and his wife Wilhelmina Carter, about 26, had children John, Sallie and Mary. (She is a Carter by birth, as her son's death record shows, but no link to Michael's Kent County Carters is known.) The Maryland State Archives' death index cards (series SE58) list other Glandens nearby who may be kin. William H. Glanden died in Queen Anne's County on 20 September 1900, aged 40, and a little Ida Glanden, aged 2, died there on 16 October 1899, perhaps his daughter. David Glanding died in Baltimore on 2 October 1899, aged 74, old enough to be George W.'s father or older brother. None of them is linked yet.

stories.title: John Henry Glanding (1863–1919) and Mary Lena Hunter of Caroline County
stories.group: The Passwaters, Adamses, Glandings and Hunters (the Eastern Shore lines)
stories.html:
Their son John Henry Glanding was born on 28 February 1863. He married Mary Lena Hunter, daughter of Joseph Hunter and Mary Rebecca Enbert. She was born on 13 November 1880, so she was seventeen years younger than John, and only eighteen when their first son, George Leonard, was born at Bridgetown on 20 May 1899. Nora Mary followed in 1901 (at Goldsboro), then Oscar, Anna Elizabeth (1911) and, last, Elise Rebecca, on 15 October 1918.

John, a farmer, died near Greensboro on 23 November 1919, when Elise was one. His death certificate, given by "Mrs. Mary L. Glanden" of Henderson, names his parents as Geo. W. Glanden and Wilhemina Carter. Mary Lena raised the five children alone; in 1920 she was a widow in Caroline County with all of them at home. She later lived in Ridgely, on First Avenue West in 1950. She died on 18 March 1965 and was buried in Greensboro Cemetery, where John lies.

Sources: 1850, 1870, 1880 censuses; James E. Passwaters' 1921 death certificate; U.S. Civil War soldiers index; 6th Delaware Infantry history; Margaret Ellen Passwater's Maryland death index; 1860, 1870, 1920, 1940, 1950 censuses for the Glandings; Maryland birth and death indexes for John H. Glanding, Mary Lena Glanding and their children; Mary L. Glanding's headstone.

stories.title: Kate Bleakley: the aunt who knew Edgar Allan Poe
stories.group: Side quests
stories.html:
Kate Bleakley was very likely the older sister of Michael's 4th great-grandmother Louisa (Blakely) Raphun. In old age she told a Baltimore newspaper that the young Edgar Allan Poe had written her love letters.

The aunt and the poet. A month after the Colonel's death, on 2 March 1903, an old Baltimore lady named Mrs. Kate Henderson turned 87 at her home, 903 North Fulton Avenue. A reporter from the Baltimore Morning Herald came to see her, and the paper ran the story the next day under the headline "Was the Sweetheart of Edgar Allan Poe." It called her an aunt of the late Col. Charles W. Raphun.

Kate said she was born on 2 March 1816 in a house at the corner of Lombard Street and Marsh Market Space. She had lived in Baltimore all her life apart from a short stay in Philadelphia. She married three times, to a Mr. Payne, a Mr. Spangler and lastly a Mr. Henderson, who had died about forty years before. She had outlived all her children.

She told the reporter, modestly and only when pressed, that Poe had been an intimate friend. While he was a cadet at West Point (1830–31), he wrote her letters declaring his love and sent her little poems. A married daughter later took the letters to New Orleans, where they were treasured. After that daughter died, they were never found. According to the Poe Society's notes, Kate told a later paper that she had never really been Poe's sweetheart.

Poe in Baltimore. The dates fit Poe's life. He came to Baltimore in May 1829, just out of the army, poor and trying to publish his poems. His older brother Henry lived with their aunt, Maria Clemm. Poe went to Richmond early in 1830, and in June 1830 he entered West Point, giving a false age. He soon wanted out. In January 1831 he stopped going to formations and classes on purpose, was court-martialed on 28 January and dismissed. By May 1831 he was back in Baltimore, living with Mrs. Clemm, his bedridden grandmother, his little cousin Virginia (later his wife) and Henry, who died that August. Kate was 13 when Poe first came to Baltimore and 15 when he came back from West Point (American Heritage, "Cadet Edgar Allan Poe").

Why this fits our family. The paper never gave Kate's maiden name. The Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore, working only from her birth date and birthplace, identified her as Kate Bleakley/Blakely. Baltimore directories of 1822–23 list Matthew Blakeley, tavern keeper and grocer, at the corner of Water Street and Marsh Market Space, steps from where Kate said she was born. The Society did not know about our family. But the FamilySearch tree, made separately, gives Louisa Raphun's parents as Mathew Blakely and Ann Brown. So Kate and Louisa were very likely sisters, daughters of Matthew Blakely, and that is exactly why the paper called Kate the Colonel's aunt.

A Poe biographer knew her too. There is a third witness, independent of both. Hervey Allen's biography of Poe, Israfel (1926, revised 1934), names her. One of the first glimpses of Poe after he came back to Baltimore in 1831, Allen writes, is of him calling on "Kate Bleakely" in full cadet uniform, with his brother Henry. Allen says her father, Matthew Bleakley, kept the Armistead Hotel on Short Swan Street; that Kate was probably one of Henry's sweethearts; and that Poe later wrote verses to her (Israfel, ch. 15, pp. 258–259). Allen puts the visit after West Point, not during it, and says nothing about letters. So Kate's story of love letters from the Point may have grown a little over seventy years. But a Poe biographer knew of Poe calling on her, and knew her father was Matthew, which is the name the FamilySearch tree gives for Louisa's father.

How sure: the 1903 article and the 1880 census are records. Louisa's parents come from another tree, and Kate's maiden name is the Poe Society's inference. Two independent lines of evidence point to the same Blakely family, which makes it probable.

This side quest comes from the family story Kate (Blakely) Henderson (1816–?): the Colonel's aunt who knew Poe.

stories.title: Lewis Robards, Rachel Donelson and Andrew Jackson
stories.group: Side quests
stories.html:
The half-uncle in the history books. William Jr.'s half-brother Capt. Lewis Robards (1758–1814), a fellow Revolutionary veteran, married a 17-year-old named Rachel Donelson at Harrodsburg on 1 March 1785. The marriage was unhappy. Rachel went back to her family near Nashville, where she met a young lawyer named Andrew Jackson. She and Jackson married believing Lewis had gotten a divorce, but the divorce wasn't final until 1793, and they had to marry again in 1794. Nearly forty years later, in the 1828 presidential election, Jackson's opponents made Rachel's "bigamy" a national scandal. She died that December, just before Jackson took office, and he always blamed his enemies for it. Lewis remarried and had ten children with Hannah Winn. His brother George and mother Elizabeth appear in our 1805 will.

This side quest comes from the family story William Robards Sr. (about 1729–1783): 6,000 acres in Kentucky, and Andrew Jackson's rival.

stories.title: Jack Jouett's ride and the Robards aunt who married him
stories.group: Side quests
stories.html:
The half-aunt who married a hero of the Revolution. Lewis's sister Sally Robards married Jack Jouett. Jouett is famous for his ride of June 1781: he galloped about 40 miles through the night over back roads to warn Thomas Jefferson and the Virginia legislature that British cavalry under Banastre Tarleton was coming to capture them. Jefferson escaped Monticello with minutes to spare. Jack and Sally settled in Kentucky, and their son Matthew Harris Jouett became Kentucky's best-known portrait painter; he painted Lafayette. Elizabeth Robards's 1805 will mentions a colt she had given to a George Jouett.

stories.title: Barnett Rogers at Blue Licks, beside Daniel Boone's son
stories.group: Side quests
stories.html:
Barnett (Bernard) Rogers was an uncle of Kristin's 5th great-grandmother Elizabeth Rogers, the little girl inside Bryan's Station. He rode out with Daniel Boone to chase the raiders, and like Boone's son Israel he did not come back.

Blue Licks, 19 August 1782. About 182 mounted militia gathered at Bryan's Station and chased the raiders northeast along the old buffalo trace to the salt springs at the Lower Blue Licks on the Licking River. Colonel John Todd had the command. Lieutenant Colonel Daniel Boone led the Fayette men, and Colonels Stephen Trigg and Hugh McGary the Lincoln County men. Colonel Benjamin Logan was a day behind with hundreds more. At the river, Boone, who knew the ground, warned that the open trail looked like an ambush and urged them to wait for Logan. Before the officers could agree, McGary spurred his horse into the ford with the shout remembered as "Them that ain't cowards, follow me!" and the men poured across after him.

On the ridge beyond, Caldwell's warriors were hidden in the ravines. The fight lasted perhaps fifteen minutes. The center and right broke within about five. Todd and Trigg were shot dead. Boone's son Israel, about 23, was shot through the neck at his father's side, and Boone had to leave his body and run for the ford. At the river Benjamin Netherland rallied a few men for a volley that checked the pursuit long enough for survivors to swim the Licking. Boone counted 77 Kentuckians killed and a dozen wounded, and several more were carried off as prisoners. About two of every five men who rode out never came home. Among the officers killed was "Lieutenant Barnett Rogers," our John's brother, named on the Blue Licks roll of honor alongside Col. John Todd, Col. Stephen Trigg and Maj. Silas Harlan.

Days later Logan arrived with about 460 men. With Boone they went back to the battlefield and buried the dead they could find in a common grave, by Boone's count 43 bodies; the rest were never found. The Rogers family history says Barnett's body was instead carried home and buried in the old Rogers graveyard at Bryan's Station, under a marked stone. Barnett had made his will two years earlier, in Culpeper, on 30 October 1780; it was proved there on 20 January 1783 and left his property to his brothers William and Joseph and his sisters.

This side quest comes from the family story Bryan's Station and Blue Licks, 1782: the Rogers brothers in the last fight of the Revolution.

stories.title: John Woolman: Tamar's cousin who spoke against slavery
stories.group: Side quests
stories.html:
The cousin who spoke against slavery. Esther's brother Samuel Woolman named his first son John, born on the Rancocas farm on 19 October 1720. That John Woolman, Tamar's first cousin, became one of the first and most persistent voices against slavery in America. As a young clerk in Mount Holly, about 23, he was asked by his employer to write a bill of sale for an enslaved woman. He wrote it, said it troubled him, and after that he refused to write any will or bill of sale that passed people on as property. He became a tailor so that he could travel, and for nearly thirty years he went on foot and horseback among Friends from New England to the Carolinas, sitting with slaveholders and telling them, gently and plainly, that keeping people as property was wrong. When he stayed in a slaveholder's house he paid the enslaved people who waited on him. He published Some Considerations on the Keeping of Negroes in 1754 and a second part in 1762. In 1776 Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, which included Tamar's Nottingham meeting, ruled that Friends who still held slaves would be disowned, and Woolman's long campaign is a large part of why. He wore undyed clothes and refused silver dishes, and he crossed to England in 1772 in steerage, living with the sailors. He caught smallpox and died at York on 7 October 1772. His Journal, published in 1774, has never gone out of print and was chosen for the first volume of the Harvard Classics.

This side quest comes from the family story Tamar Allen's Quaker roots: the Bortons of Aynho, the Woolmans of Painswick, and a cousin who spoke against slavery.

stories.title: Aaron Burr's treason trial and the Underwood in the jury pool
stories.group: Side quests
stories.html:
In 1807 the former vice president Aaron Burr stood trial at Richmond for treason, accused of plotting to carve an empire out of the western territories. Chief Justice John Marshall presided, and on 1 September the jury found him not guilty; a second trial on a lesser charge followed that month. Picking jurors who hadn't already made up their minds was nearly impossible, because the whole country had been reading about the plot for a year. One of the men called was very likely the brother of Kristin's 6th great-grandmother Hannah Underwood. (Burr turns up in family lore too: Marion County, Kentucky tradition says he once stopped at Daniel Everhart's house near Lebanon, though that's a legend, not a record.)

The uncle on Aaron Burr's jury panel. William Robards Jr.'s wife, Elizabeth Lewis, was the daughter of William Lewis and Hannah Underwood of Goochland. Hannah's brother was very likely Thomas Underwood, a Goochland planter and merchant of the "Lickinhole" plantation. Before the Revolution he ran up a debt of more than £2,000 to the London merchants John Norton & Sons, and William Lewis stood as one of his securities. In 1790 Thomas wrote that he would move to Kentucky once his affairs were settled. In September 1807, when Aaron Burr was tried in Richmond, "Thomas Underwood, sen." was called in the jury pool. Burr himself challenged him, arguing that Underwood already had an unfavorable opinion of him, and Underwood agreed that he did, so he was excused. So Burr turns up in this family too.

This side quest comes from the family story William Robards Sr. (about 1729–1783): 6,000 acres in Kentucky, and Andrew Jackson's rival.
